◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Power Automate is Microsoft's automation platform — formerly called Microsoft Flow. It connects services, automates repetitive tasks, and ranges from simple email triggers to enterprise RPA. The PL-100, PL-200, and PL-500 exams all test Power Automate concepts.

What Power Automate is

Power Automate = Microsoft's low-code automation platform

History:
 Originally called "Microsoft Flow" (2016)
 Renamed to "Power Automate" in 2019

What it does:
 - Trigger workflows on events (email arrives, item created, scheduled time)
 - Connect to 1000+ services via connectors
 - Run multi-step actions in sequence or in parallel
 - Handle approvals, notifications, data sync
 - Robotic Process Automation (RPA) for desktop / legacy apps
 - AI-powered actions (form processing, sentiment analysis)

Position in Power Platform:
 Power Apps — build apps
 Power Automate — automate processes
 Power BI — analyze data
 Power Pages — external-facing websites
 Power Virtual Agents — chatbots
 All share connectors and integrate via Dataverse

Types of flows

TypeTriggered byRuns on
Cloud flow — AutomatedEvent (email, item, etc.)Microsoft cloud
Cloud flow — InstantManual button / Power AppsMicrosoft cloud
Cloud flow — ScheduledCalendar (e.g., daily at 9am)Microsoft cloud
Desktop flow (RPA)Manual or from cloud flowWindows PC
Business process flowStage progression in DataverseDataverse (Model-Driven)

Anatomy of a flow

FLOW STRUCTURE
TRIGGER: the event that starts the flow (one per flow)
  Example: "When an email arrives in Outlook"

ACTIONS: the steps that run after the trigger (one or many)
  Example: "Save attachment to OneDrive" → "Send Teams message"

CONTROL: branching, looping, error-handling (optional)
  Example: "If sender is from VIP list, then notify on phone" 
Trigger:
 Always the first step
 Defines WHEN the flow runs
 Connector-specific (SharePoint, Outlook, Teams, scheduler, manual button)

Actions:
 Each step is one operation
 Output of one step is available to all subsequent steps
 Sequential by default; parallel branches possible

Connectors:
 Same as Power Apps — Standard and Premium tiers
 Each connector exposes triggers + actions

Control flow:
 Condition (if/then/else)
 Switch (multi-branch)
 Apply to each (loop)
 Do until
 Scope (group steps)
 Parallel branch (run side-by-side)

Variables:
 Initialize variable (Integer, String, Boolean, Array, Object, Float)
 Set / Increment / Decrement
 Append to array / Append to string

Where to build flows

make.powerautomate.com — main authoring portal

Or embedded:
 - Within Power Apps Studio (flow connected to canvas app)
 - Microsoft Teams (Power Automate app in Teams)
 - SharePoint (right-click list/item → Automate)
 - Excel Online (Automate menu)

The portal is the canonical way:
 Left nav:
 Home, My flows, Create, Templates, Connectors, Solutions
 Top right:
 Environment switcher

To create:
 + Create → choose flow type
 Pick a trigger
 Add actions
 Save and Test

Templates

Microsoft provides hundreds of pre-built flow templates

Find:
 make.powerautomate.com → Templates
 Search by service, scenario, or category

Popular templates:
 - "Save Office 365 email attachments to OneDrive"
 - "Get notification when a Teams message contains a keyword"
 - "Approve documents in SharePoint"
 - "Track outlook emails to Excel Online"
 - "Tweet when an RSS feed updates"
 - "Create planner task when an email arrives"

Workflow:
 Pick template → connect required services → optionally customize → save
 Saves weeks of manual setup
 Good starting point for learning

Categories:
 - Productivity (email, calendar, files)
 - Approval (sign-offs, requests)
 - Notifications (alerts, reminders)
 - Data collection (forms, surveys)
 - Backup and sync

Power Automate licensing

LicenseIncludes
Microsoft 365 (basic)Standard connectors; cloud flows; limited per-user runs
Power Automate per UserUnlimited flows; premium connectors; ~$15/user
Power Automate per FlowPer-flow plan (~$100/flow/month); for high-volume
Power Automate PremiumIncludes RPA, AI Builder, hosted machines
Process MiningAnalyze process patterns; premium add-on

Run limits

Power Automate enforces request limits per license

Microsoft 365 plans:
 ~2000 requests/day per user typical
 Each step in a flow = 1 request (roughly)

Premium licenses:
 Much higher: 40,000+ requests/day per user

Performance considerations:
 Each action call counts
 Apply to each loop with 100 items = 100+ requests
 Be mindful in high-volume scenarios

Throttling:
 If exceeded, flow runs slow or pause
 Some retries automatic
 Best to design efficient flows from start

Use cases

Personal productivity:
 - Save email attachments to OneDrive
 - Forward important emails to Teams
 - Track favorite tweets to a sheet
 - Daily reminders

Team workflows:
 - Approve documents
 - Notify on SharePoint changes
 - Sync Planner tasks to calendar
 - Onboarding checklists

Business processes:
 - Invoice approvals
 - Lead routing
 - Customer onboarding
 - Document generation

Enterprise automation (with RPA):
 - Data entry between legacy and modern apps
 - Bulk record updates
 - Report generation
 - System migrations

AI-augmented:
 - Extract data from invoices
 - Translate emails
 - Detect sentiment
 - Generate summaries

Power Automate vs Power Apps

Power AppsPower Automate
User-facing apps with screensBackground workflows; no UI
User initiates interactionsTriggers run automatically
Forms, galleries, navigationConditions, loops, branches
Power Fx formulasWDL / Expression language
Builds the experienceBuilds the orchestration

They work together: Power Apps button → triggers Power Automate flow → flow does the work → returns result.

Worked example — first flow

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Save attachments to OneDrive
// Goal: when an email arrives with an attachment, save attachment to OneDrive

// Step 1: Go to make.powerautomate.com
// Step 2: + Create → Automated cloud flow
// Step 3: Name: "Save Email Attachments"
// Step 4: Choose trigger: "When a new email arrives (V3)" - Outlook
// Step 5: Click Create

// Step 6: Configure trigger
// Folder: Inbox
// Importance: Any (or High only)
// Has Attachment: Yes (filter)
// Include Attachments: Yes

// Step 7: Add action below trigger
// + New step → "Apply to each"
// Select output from previous: Attachments
// This loops through each attachment

// Step 8: Inside "Apply to each"
// + Add action → "Create file" (OneDrive for Business)
// Folder Path: /Email Attachments/
// File Name: [Name] from dynamic content
// File Content: [Content] from dynamic content

// Step 9: Save the flow
// Click Save (top right)
// Test → "Manually trigger" or wait for matching email

// Step 10: Monitor runs
// My flows → click flow → Run history
// See success/failure of each run

Common Power Automate mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Wrong flow type — automated vs instant vs scheduled mismatch
  2. Trigger conditions skipped — flow runs on every event, costing requests
  3. Missing connection auth — flow fails on first run
  4. Hardcoded values in dynamic content scenarios
  5. Apply to each over a single record — unnecessary loop
  6. No error handling — silent failures or retry storms
  7. Storing secrets in flow — use Key Vault / connection refs
  8. Mixing premium and standard connectors without realizing license impact
  9. Run limit exceeded — flow throttled; consider Premium
  10. No testing before deploy — flow takes wrong action on real data
★ ON THE EXAM

"Power Automate's previous name?" → Microsoft Flow.

"Authoring portal?" → make.powerautomate.com.

"Cloud flow types?" → Automated, Instant, Scheduled.

"RPA flow?" → Desktop flow.

"Trigger?" → The event that starts the flow (one per flow).

"Action?" → A step that runs after the trigger.

"Control flow?" → Condition, Switch, Apply to each, Do until, Scope.

"Where to find templates?" → make.powerautomate.com → Templates.

"Run history?" → My flows → flow → Run history.

"Premium needed for?" → Premium connectors, RPA, AI Builder.

"Standard with M365?" → SharePoint, Outlook, Teams, OneDrive triggers/actions.

"Multi-step flow?" → Sequential or parallel branches.

"Manual trigger?" → Instant flow (button or Power Apps trigger).

"Scheduled run?" → Scheduled cloud flow.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Power Automate is Microsoft's low-code automation platform (formerly Microsoft Flow)
  • Three cloud flow types: Automated (event-triggered), Instant (manual), Scheduled (time-based)
  • Desktop flows (RPA) automate Windows applications
  • Every flow has one Trigger and one-or-many Actions
  • Authoring portal: make.powerautomate.com
  • Connectors are shared with Power Apps: Standard (M365) and Premium tiers
  • 1000+ connectors available; Microsoft + third-party partners build them
  • Templates provide pre-built starting points for common scenarios
  • Control structures: Condition, Switch, Apply to each, Do until, Scope, Parallel branch
  • Microsoft 365 includes basic Power Automate with standard connectors
  • Premium licenses needed for premium connectors, RPA, AI Builder
  • Each step typically counts as one "request"; daily limits enforced
  • Power Automate + Power Apps work together: app button → flow → action
  • Run history shows success/failure per flow run; key for debugging
  • Common uses: notifications, approvals, file sync, data integration, RPA

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Power Automate has two distinct execution models: cloud flows (running on Microsoft's servers, talking to APIs) and desktop flows (running on a Windows PC, controlling the UI). They solve different problems. The PL-100 and PL-500 exams test the distinction.

Cloud flows

Cloud flows run in Microsoft's data centers
 
Architecture:
 Trigger (event) → Power Automate cloud → Actions (API calls)
 No local installation needed
 
Connect to:
 Cloud services with APIs (Microsoft 365, Salesforce, ServiceNow, etc.)
 REST APIs via HTTP action
 Webhooks
 Other Microsoft cloud services

Subtypes:
 Automated — triggered by an event in a connector
 Instant — triggered by user action (button or Power Apps)
 Scheduled — triggered by a calendar schedule

Strengths:
 - Reliable; runs 24/7 in the cloud
 - Scalable; Microsoft handles infrastructure
 - Integrates with 1000+ connectors
 - Multi-step workflows easy
 - Approvals, notifications, complex logic

Limitations:
 - Only works with services that have APIs / connectors
 - Cannot interact with desktop applications
 - Cannot scrape websites without API
 - Cannot type into legacy software with no API

Desktop flows (RPA)

Desktop flows = Robotic Process Automation (RPA)
 Runs on a Windows machine via Power Automate Desktop (PAD)
 Controls applications by simulating user actions

Two modes:
 Attended:
 Runs while user is logged in
 User sees the flow execute
 Good for: assisting workers, demos, one-off automations

 Unattended:
 Runs on a machine without user supervision
 Power Automate Premium required + machine designated as "unattended"
 Good for: 24/7 batch automation, scheduled bulk processing

Architecture:
 Desktop flow on Windows PC → controls apps via UI automation
 Records: mouse clicks, keyboard, text fields, dropdowns
 Reads: window titles, control properties, OCR text

Connect to:
 ANY Windows app: Excel, browser, SAP GUI, legacy mainframes, custom apps
 No API needed; just the UI

Power Automate Desktop is free on Windows 10/11

Cloud vs Desktop comparison

Cloud flowDesktop flow (RPA)
Runs in Microsoft cloudRuns on Windows PC
API-drivenUI-driven (mouse/keyboard)
Works with cloud servicesWorks with any Windows app
Reliable; auto-retryBrittle; UI changes break it
Fast (seconds)Slower (mimics human speed)
Free with M365Free attended; Premium for unattended
Built in browserBuilt in Power Automate Desktop app

When to use which

Use Cloud Flow when:
 ✓ Source/destination has APIs (M365, Salesforce, SQL, etc.)
 ✓ Need 24/7 reliability
 ✓ Multi-step workflows with approvals
 ✓ Event-driven (new email, item created, schedule)
 ✓ Webhook-based integrations

Use Desktop Flow when:
 ✓ App has NO API (legacy system, custom internal tool)
 ✓ Need to interact with desktop applications
 ✓ Web scraping (when APIs don't exist)
 ✓ Excel macros that interact with windows
 ✓ Replicating manual user steps

Use Both when:
 - Cloud flow handles cloud parts
 - Desktop flow handles legacy app
 - Cloud flow calls desktop flow as a sub-process
 - Example: Cloud flow gets new request → Desktop flow enters into legacy system → Cloud flow notifies user

This hybrid pattern is common in enterprise scenarios

Power Automate Desktop (PAD)

Power Automate Desktop = standalone Windows app for RPA

Installation:
 Free with Windows 10/11
 Download: powerautomate.microsoft.com/desktop
 Sign in with Microsoft 365 account

Interface (different from cloud flow designer):
 Left: Action library (400+ actions)
 Center: Flow workspace (sequential steps)
 Right: Variables panel
 Bottom: Subflows tabs

Build flows by:
 1. Drag actions from library
 2. Configure parameters
 3. Or use Recorder (record mouse + keyboard)
 4. Test by running
 5. Debug step-by-step

Recorder modes:
 Desktop recorder: clicks, keys, window navigation
 Web recorder: browser automation (with browser extension)

Save:
 Local: just on this PC
 Cloud: synced to Power Automate (premium for cloud sync)

Desktop flow action categories

UI Automation:
 - Click on UI element
 - Get details of UI element
 - Set text in UI element
 - Wait for element

Variables:
 - Set variable
 - Increment/Decrement
 - Convert types
 - Get text length

Conditionals:
 - If / Else if / Else
 - Switch / Case

Loops:
 - Loop (counter)
 - For each (in collection)
 - Loop while

System:
 - Run application
 - Wait for process
 - Show message dialog
 - Get system date/time

Mouse and keyboard:
 - Click mouse
 - Send keys
 - Move mouse to coordinates

Browser:
 - Launch new browser instance
 - Navigate to URL
 - Click element on page
 - Get element value
 - Run JavaScript

Excel:
 - Launch Excel
 - Read from Excel
 - Write to Excel
 - Run macro

File and folder:
 - Copy file
 - Move file
 - List files in folder
 - Delete file

OCR:
 - Recognize text from image
 - Used when no proper UI handles exist

Email, FTP, HTTP, SQL, etc.:
 - Many service interactions even from desktop

Building a cloud-desktop hybrid

Pattern: cloud flow orchestrates desktop flow

Setup:
 1. Build a desktop flow in PAD
 2. Save and publish to your tenant
 3. Cloud flow → Add action → "Power Automate Desktop" connector
 4. Action: "Run a flow built with Power Automate Desktop"
 5. Select target machine and desktop flow
 6. Pass input parameters

Triggers for hybrid flows:
 - Schedule (run nightly)
 - Email received (process request)
 - Power Apps button (user-triggered)
 - Approval result (after manager approves)

Machine modes:
 Attended: user logged in, machine in normal use
 Unattended: dedicated VM or PC, no user, fully automated
 Machine group: pool of unattended machines for load balancing

Example workflow:
 Cloud flow: nightly schedule
 1. Query Dataverse for pending records
 2. For each record, call desktop flow
 Desktop flow: opens legacy app, enters data, saves
 3. Update Dataverse with status
 4. Send summary email to admin

This pattern enables automating across cloud + on-prem + legacy

Worked example — cloud flow + desktop flow

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Hybrid invoice processing
// Goal: process invoices arriving via email; enter into legacy accounting system

// Cloud flow:
// Trigger: When new email with attachment arrives in Outlook
// Conditions: From "vendor@example.com" AND has attachment
// 
// Actions:
// 1. Save attachment (PDF invoice) to OneDrive
// 2. AI Builder → Extract invoice data from PDF (premium)
// → returns: vendor name, amount, invoice number, date
// 3. Create Dataverse record with extracted data
// 4. Run desktop flow → "Enter invoice in legacy app"
// Pass: invoice number, vendor, amount, date as inputs
// 5. Wait for desktop flow to complete
// 6. Update Dataverse record: status = Entered
// 7. Email: notification with summary

// Desktop flow:
// Input parameters: invoice number, vendor, amount, date
// Actions:
// 1. Launch legacy app (run AccountingApp.exe)
// 2. Wait for window "Accounting Suite"
// 3. Click "New Invoice" button
// 4. Fill fields:
// - Vendor field: type vendor
// - Invoice number: type invoice number
// - Amount: type amount
// - Date: type date
// 5. Click "Save"
// 6. Capture confirmation number (OCR or read text field)
// 7. Close app
// 8. Return confirmation number as output

// Result: invoice goes from email → cloud → legacy system → confirmation
// without manual data entry

Common cloud/desktop mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Trying desktop flow when API exists — cloud flow more reliable
  2. Trying cloud flow when no API — must use desktop RPA
  3. Desktop flow against changing UI — UI updates break flow; use stable selectors
  4. Unattended without premium license — won't run; needs license
  5. Hardcoded credentials in desktop flow — store securely
  6. No error handling in desktop flow — silent stuck
  7. OCR for things that should use API — slow and unreliable
  8. Premium connector in M365-only license — flow fails on connector
  9. Multiple desktop flows on one machine conflicting — coordinate carefully
  10. No timeout on UI waits — flow stuck if element never appears
★ ON THE EXAM

"Cloud flow runs where?" → Microsoft cloud / data centers.

"Desktop flow runs where?" → Windows PC (with Power Automate Desktop installed).

"RPA?" → Robotic Process Automation; desktop flows.

"Power Automate Desktop is free?" → Yes, on Windows 10/11.

"Attended vs Unattended?" → Attended needs user logged in; Unattended runs alone (premium).

"Cloud flow can?" → Talk to APIs of cloud services.

"Desktop flow can?" → Click UI elements, type into windows, scrape screens.

"Hybrid pattern?" → Cloud flow calls desktop flow for legacy parts.

"No API available?" → Use desktop flow (RPA).

"24/7 automation?" → Cloud flow (or unattended desktop on dedicated machine).

"Web scraping?" → Desktop flow's browser actions (or HTTP cloud action if structured).

"Excel automation?" → Cloud flow uses Excel Online connector; Desktop flow controls Excel on PC.

"Action library size?" → Cloud has 1000+ connector actions; Desktop has 400+ actions.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Cloud flows run in Microsoft's cloud, calling APIs of connected services
  • Desktop flows (RPA) run on Windows PCs, controlling apps via UI automation
  • Power Automate Desktop is the Windows app for building/running desktop flows
  • Free for use on Windows 10/11; premium for cloud sync and unattended
  • Three cloud flow types: Automated, Instant, Scheduled
  • Two desktop flow modes: Attended (user logged in) and Unattended (no user; needs premium)
  • Cloud strengths: 24/7, scalable, API-driven, multi-connector workflows
  • Desktop strengths: works with any Windows app, including legacy without APIs
  • Hybrid pattern: cloud orchestrates; desktop handles legacy steps
  • Action categories in PAD: UI automation, variables, conditionals, loops, mouse/keyboard, browser, Excel, file, OCR
  • Recording features in PAD: Desktop recorder + Web recorder for browser
  • Desktop flows are more brittle (UI changes break them) than cloud flows
  • Use cloud when APIs exist; use desktop only when needed
  • Premium license required for: unattended desktop flows, premium connectors, AI Builder
  • Machines for desktop flows: register via Power Automate; can group as load-balanced pools

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Triggers and actions are the atoms of any flow. Every flow has exactly one trigger and one or more actions. The PL-100 exam tests recognizing trigger types, common actions, and their configuration patterns.

Trigger types in cloud flows

TypeExamplesUse case
Polling"When item is created (SharePoint)"Detect changes in services without webhooks
Webhook (push)"When email arrives (Outlook)"Service pushes event to flow instantly
Schedule"Recurrence: every 1 day at 9am"Periodic batch jobs
Manual / Instant"For a selected item / Manually trigger / Power Apps button"User initiates flow
Sub-flow / Child"When a flow is invoked"Called from another flow

Polling triggers

Some connectors don't support push notifications
Power Automate "polls" the service periodically

Example: SharePoint "When an item is created"
 Power Automate checks the list every 5-15 seconds (free tier; faster on premium)
 Compares last check to new items
 Triggers for each new item

Latency:
 Free: up to 15 min initially; typically 5-15 sec on premium
 Limit: 1 poll per second on premium

Cost:
 Each polling check counts toward request limits
 More frequent polling = more requests

Common polling triggers:
 - SharePoint: "When an item is created/modified"
 - Microsoft Forms: "When a new response is submitted"
 - Excel Online: "When a new row is added to a table" (limited; not always reliable)
 - Database queries on a schedule

Avoid:
 Polling extremely frequently for low-value events
 Use webhooks where available

Webhook triggers

Webhook = service pushes event to Power Automate immediately
 Near-instant trigger (under 1 second typically)
 More efficient (no polling needed)

Common webhook triggers:
 - Outlook: "When a new email arrives"
 - Teams: "When a new message is added to a channel"
 - Dataverse: "When a row is added/modified/deleted"
 - SharePoint: "When a file is created" (some)
 - HTTP webhook: "When an HTTP request is received" (custom)

Setup:
 Connector handles webhook subscription automatically
 When flow saved, Power Automate registers webhook with the service
 When event occurs, service POSTs to Power Automate
 Power Automate runs the flow

Best practice:
 Prefer webhook triggers over polling
 Faster + cheaper

Manual triggers

User-initiated; not event-driven

Types:
 1. "Manually trigger a flow"
 - User clicks Run in Power Automate
 - Optional inputs (text, number, file, etc.)
 - Good for one-off jobs

 2. "For a selected item / file / row"
 - From SharePoint, Excel, OneDrive UI
 - User right-clicks → Automate → runs flow on that item

 3. "Power Apps (V2)"
 - Power Apps button calls this flow
 - Inputs defined; outputs returned
 - Common Power Apps + Power Automate integration

 4. "Button" (mobile / Flow button)
 - Tap to run from Power Automate mobile app

Use cases:
 - Manual approvals (start the approval flow on demand)
 - One-off cleanup tasks
 - Power Apps users triggering complex backend logic
 - Quick reports / data exports

Scheduled triggers

"Recurrence" trigger
Defines a schedule for the flow

Configuration:
 Frequency: Second / Minute / Hour / Day / Week / Month
 Interval: how many of that unit
 Time zone: which TZ for "9am"
 Start time: when to begin
 On these days: filter by weekdays
 At these hours / minutes: filter by clock time

Examples:
 Every Monday at 9am
 Every 30 minutes during business hours (9am-5pm)
 First day of each month at midnight
 Every 5 minutes (frequent polling)

Limits:
 Minimum frequency: 1 minute (free); some plans allow seconds
 Each run counts as a flow execution
 Many scheduled flows + frequent intervals = high cost

Use cases:
 - Nightly data exports
 - Weekly reports
 - Periodic cleanup
 - Polling APIs that don't have triggers

Trigger conditions

Filter so flow only runs for matching events
Reduces unnecessary runs

Set via:
 Trigger step → ... menu → Settings → Trigger Conditions

Format:
 Expression returning true/false
 WDL syntax (similar to Office UI Fabric expressions)

Examples:
 Only run for VIP customers:
 @equals(triggerOutputs()?['body/customerTier'], 'VIP')

 Only run for high-priority items:
 @greater(triggerOutputs()?['body/priority'], 5)

 Combine:
 @and(
 equals(triggerOutputs()?['body/status'], 'New'),
 equals(triggerOutputs()?['body/region'], 'East')
 )

Without trigger conditions:
 Flow runs on EVERY matching trigger event
 Each step counts toward request limits
 Wastes resources

With trigger conditions:
 Flow skips before any actions
 Only runs when condition is true
 Much more efficient

Trade-off:
 More complex setup
 Harder to debug (failed conditions don't show in run history)

Actions overview

An action = one step in the flow after the trigger

Categories:
 Connector actions:
 - Office 365 Outlook: Send email, Get emails
 - SharePoint: Get items, Create item, Update item
 - Dataverse: List rows, Add row, Update row
 - Office 365 Users: Get user profile
 - Teams: Post message, Create channel
 - HTTP: Custom REST call
 - And many more (1000+ connectors)

 Control actions:
 - Condition (if/then/else)
 - Switch (multi-branch)
 - Apply to each (loop)
 - Do until (conditional loop)
 - Scope (group)
 - Parallel branch
 - Terminate (end flow with status)

 Variables:
 - Initialize variable
 - Set variable
 - Increment / Decrement
 - Append to string / array

 Data operations:
 - Compose (set value)
 - Filter array
 - Select (transform array)
 - Join (concatenate)
 - Parse JSON
 - Create CSV / HTML table

 Schedule:
 - Delay (wait N units)
 - Delay until (wait for specific time)

Each action takes:
 Inputs: configuration + dynamic values from previous steps
 Outputs: data available to subsequent steps

Dynamic content

Dynamic content = output of previous steps available to current

How it appears:
 Click in any input field
 Right-side panel shows "Dynamic Content"
 Lists all available values from earlier steps
 Click to insert as token

Examples:
 Trigger output: Email Subject, Email Body, Sender Email
 Action output: Created Item ID, Created Item URL, etc.

Inserting:
 Token appears as a colored "pill" in the field
 Power Automate substitutes the actual value at runtime

Mixed text:
 Email body: "Hello @{triggerOutputs()?['body/Sender']}, your request..."
 Or: type "Hello " then click dynamic content to insert sender

Common dynamic content:
 Trigger: body, header values, IDs, names
 Get items: Returns array; access via Apply to each
 Compose: Outputs (the value you set)
 Variables: variable's current value

When to use dynamic content vs expressions:
 Dynamic content: simple references
 Expressions: transformations (concat, formats, dates math)

Expressions

Power Automate has its own expression language

Click "Expression" tab in dynamic content panel
Or use @{expression} syntax directly

Common functions:

String:
 concat(s1, s2, ...)
 substring(s, start, length)
 toUpper(s), toLower(s)
 replace(s, old, new)
 trim(s)
 split(s, separator)

Number:
 add(a, b), sub(a, b), mul(a, b), div(a, b)
 mod(a, b)
 min(a, b), max(a, b)

Date:
 utcNow()
 formatDateTime(date, 'yyyy-MM-dd')
 addDays(date, n)
 ticks(date)

Logical:
 equals(a, b), not(a)
 if(condition, true_val, false_val)
 and(c1, c2), or(c1, c2)

Array:
 length(array)
 first(array), last(array)
 union(a1, a2)
 intersection(a1, a2)
 contains(array, item)

JSON / Object:
 json(string)
 string(object)
 outputs('actionName')
 body('actionName')
 variables('varName')

Compose with dynamic content + expressions:
 concat('Hello ', triggerOutputs()?['body/Name'], '!')

Connection references

When you add a connector action, you select a connection

Connection = authenticated instance of the connector
Per user; uses their credentials

Multiple connections per user possible:
 - Personal email vs work email
 - Different SharePoint sites
 - Different Salesforce orgs

Connection reference (advanced):
 Abstraction layer for solution deployment
 Solution moves between environments → connection refs auto-map
 Maker doesn't need to recreate connections in target env

Service accounts:
 Common for production: shared service account for the flow
 Avoids "broken on maker leaving" scenarios
 Use Azure AD app registration or service principal

Common trigger/action mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Polling when webhook is available — slower, more cost
  2. No trigger conditions — flow runs unnecessarily
  3. Hardcoded values instead of dynamic content
  4. Wrong connector authentication — flow fails
  5. Forgetting to test with realistic data
  6. Expression syntax errors — typos in @{} cause runtime fails
  7. Missing null checks — flow fails on empty/missing fields
  8. Premium connector in non-premium flow — runtime error
  9. Connection broken after user leaves company
  10. No timeout for long-running actions — flow hangs indefinitely
★ ON THE EXAM

"How many triggers per flow?" → Exactly one.

"How many actions?" → One or many.

"Trigger types?" → Polling, Webhook, Schedule, Manual, Sub-flow.

"Filter trigger events?" → Trigger conditions.

"Where to set trigger conditions?" → Trigger ... menu → Settings.

"Push vs pull?" → Webhook = push (instant); Polling = pull (periodic).

"Schedule frequency?" → Second/Minute/Hour/Day/Week/Month.

"Output from previous step?" → Dynamic content.

"Custom transformations?" → Expressions (WDL-based language).

"Common functions?" → concat, substring, formatDateTime, addDays, equals, if.

"Insert dynamic content?" → Click input field; right panel shows available.

"Multiple connections per user?" → Yes; per-service per-account.

"Connection reference?" → Abstracts connection for ALM/solutions.

"Trigger condition format?" → Expression returning true/false.

  • Every flow has exactly ONE trigger and one-or-more actions
  • Trigger types: Polling (periodic check), Webhook (instant push), Schedule (calendar), Manual, Sub-flow
  • Webhook triggers are faster and cheaper than polling; prefer when available
  • Schedule triggers use Recurrence with frequency (second to month) and time-of-day filters
  • Manual triggers: "Manually trigger a flow", "For a selected item/file/row", "Power Apps", "Button"
  • Trigger conditions filter events before flow runs (saves cost)
  • Action categories: connectors (1000+), control flow, variables, data operations, schedule
  • Dynamic content lets you reference outputs of previous steps via UI
  • Expressions provide transformations (concat, dates, math, JSON, arrays)
  • Common expression functions: concat, formatDateTime, addDays, equals, if, length
  • Each connector action requires a connection (authenticated instance)
  • Connections are per-user with their credentials
  • Connection references enable solution portability between environments
  • Service accounts recommended for production flows (vs personal connections)
  • Test with realistic data; consider edge cases for missing/empty fields

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Automated flows are the most common type — they fire on events from connected services. Mastering automated flow patterns covers ~40% of practical Power Automate usage. The PL-100 exam tests trigger selection, configuration, and best practices.

What automated flows are

Automated flow = cloud flow triggered by an EVENT from a connector

Examples:
 - Email arrives in Outlook → file attachment to OneDrive
 - SharePoint item created → notify team
 - Forms response submitted → create Trello card
 - Dataverse row updated → call external API

Key feature: runs WITHOUT user intervention
 Service detects event → triggers Power Automate → flow runs

Triggered events typically:
 - Creation of an item (email, record, file, form response)
 - Update / modification of an item
 - Deletion (less common)
 - Approval action (within Power Automate approvals)
 - Status changes (state transitions)

Creating an automated flow

make.powerautomate.com → + Create → Automated cloud flow

Setup wizard:
 Step 1: Name your flow
 Descriptive name (e.g., "Notify on VIP email")

 Step 2: Choose trigger
 Search box for connector
 Filter by service (SharePoint, Outlook, Teams, etc.)
 Pick specific trigger

 Step 3: Click Create
 Flow editor opens
 Trigger appears as first step

 Step 4: Configure trigger
 Required parameters (folder, list, filter criteria)
 Advanced options for filtering, frequency

 Step 5: Add actions
 + New step → search for action
 Pick action; configure inputs
 Repeat for full workflow

 Step 6: Save and Test
 Save (Ctrl+S)
 Test → trigger event → verify flow runs
 Check run history for success

Common automated triggers

Office 365 Outlook:
 - "When a new email arrives (V3)"
 Options: Folder, From, To, Subject, Importance, Has Attachment, Body filter
 - "When an event is added to a calendar (V3)"
 - "When a new event is created (V3)"

SharePoint:
 - "When an item is created"
 - "When an item is modified"
 - "When an item is created or modified"
 - "When a file is created in a folder"
 - "When a file is created or modified"

Microsoft Teams:
 - "When a new message is added to a channel"
 - "When @mentioned in a channel"
 - "When a new chat message arrives"
 - "When someone is added to a team"

Microsoft Forms:
 - "When a new response is submitted"
 Note: lighter integration; designed for surveys

OneDrive for Business:
 - "When a file is created (V2)"
 - "When a file is modified (V2)"

Dataverse:
 - "When a row is added, modified, or deleted"
 Most flexible: filter by table, scope (organization/business unit/owner)
 - "When an action is performed" (process flows)

Excel Online (Business):
 - "When a row is added to a table"
 (Less reliable; SharePoint or Dataverse preferred for volume)

Power Automate native:
 - "When an HTTP request is received" — custom webhook
 - "When a flow is invoked" — sub-flow

Third-party (premium):
 - Salesforce, Dynamics, Jira, GitHub, etc.

Configuring trigger filters

Most triggers have built-in filters
Refine WHICH events fire your flow

Example: "When a new email arrives" filters:
 Folder: Inbox (default) or specific
 To: filter by recipient email
 CC, BCC
 From: filter by sender
 Subject Filter: substring match
 Importance: Any / Normal / High / Low
 Only with Attachments: Yes / No
 Body filter: text substring

Configuration tips:
 Be as specific as possible
 Each non-matching event still pulls (especially polling)
 Less specific = more cost

Trigger conditions (advanced):
 ... menu → Settings → Trigger Conditions
 Expression-based custom filter
 Runs AFTER built-in filters
 
 Example: only emails from external senders
 @not(endsWith(triggerOutputs()?['body/from'], '@mycompany.com'))

Common automated patterns

Pattern 1: Email to file storage

Trigger: When email arrives in Outlook
Filter: From specific sender / has attachment
Actions:
Apply to each attachment:
Create file in OneDrive folder
Name:Content:originalfilenameattachmentcontent
Optional:
Mark email as read
Move email to "Processed" folder
Send confirmation reply
Use case: invoice processing, receipts, document filing

Pattern 2: SharePoint to Teams notification

Trigger: When SharePoint item is created
List: Tickets / Tasks / etc.

Actions:
 Post message to Teams channel
 Message includes:
 - Item title (dynamic from trigger)
 - Link to item

 - Priority

Optional:
 Filter: only certain priority items
 Mention specific person if assigned

Use case: real-time team awareness of new work

Pattern 3: Form to Dataverse

Trigger: When new response submitted to Form
Form: Survey / Contact Request / Application

Actions:
 Get response details (extracts full data)
 Add a row in Dataverse table:
 Each form field → Dataverse column

 Notify owner / manager

Use case: customer requests, applications, surveys

Trigger: When Dataverse row is modified (e.g., Account)
Filter: status changed to "Active"

 Update related record in Salesforce
 Or: Create user in Active Directory
 Or: Post to internal system via HTTP
 Or: Update CRM/ERP

Use case: cross-system synchronization, master data sync

Trigger condition examples

VIP customer detection:
 @equals(triggerOutputs()?['body/customer_tier'], 'VIP')

External sender (not in your domain):
 @not(endsWith(triggerOutputs()?['body/from'], '@contoso.com'))

After business hours:
 @greaterOrEquals(
 hour(triggerOutputs()?['body/createdDateTime']),
 18
 )

Specific keyword in title:
 @contains(
 toLower(triggerOutputs()?['body/title']),
 'urgent'
 )

Multiple conditions combined:
 @and(
 equals(triggerOutputs()?['body/region'], 'North America'),
 greater(triggerOutputs()?['body/amount'], 10000)
 )

Recently modified (within last 5 minutes):
 @less(
 ticks(triggerOutputs()?['body/modifiedDateTime']),
 addToTime(utcNow(), -5, 'Minute')
 )

Status change only (was different):
 @not(equals(
 triggerOutputs()?['body/_status_value'],
 triggerOutputs()?['body/_oldstatus_value']
 ))

Race conditions and idempotency

When automated flow fires multiple times for same event (e.g., retries):
 Risk: duplicate actions (create record twice, send 2 emails)

Mitigations:

Idempotency keys:
 Check if already processed before acting
 Use unique key from trigger (item ID, message ID)
 
 Example:
 1. Get items in Audit table where SourceID = triggerOutputs() ID
 2. If empty (not yet processed):
 - Do the action
 - Add to Audit table
 3. If not empty:
 - Skip; already processed

Concurrency:
 By default, flows run multiple events sequentially (one at a time)
 Configurable: ... menu → Settings → Concurrency Control
 Set higher concurrency for parallel processing (faster)
 Set lower for sensitive sequences (avoid races)

Order preservation:
 Sequential by default
 No guarantee of order across multiple parallel runs
 For strict order: queue pattern with single concurrency

Common automated flow mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Trigger too broad — flow fires on irrelevant events
  2. No trigger condition for selective firing
  3. Polling overly frequent — high cost, throttled
  4. Trigger on "modify" without checking what changed — fires on every save
  5. No idempotency check — duplicate actions on retries
  6. Long flow with no error handling — partial completion on failure
  7. Tight loop: modify same record → trigger fires again → infinite loop
  8. Hard-coded user emails — break when person leaves
  9. No timeout on actions — flow hangs
  10. Premium connector in flow that should be standard — license issue
★ ON THE EXAM

"Event-driven flow type?" → Automated cloud flow.

"Create automated flow?" → make.powerautomate.com → + Create → Automated cloud flow.

"Pick trigger by?" → Connector + trigger name.

"Common email trigger?" → "When a new email arrives (V3)" - Outlook.

"Common SharePoint trigger?" → "When an item is created" or "modified".

"Filter trigger events further?" → Trigger conditions (... menu → Settings).

"Loop in flow editor?" → Apply to each.

"Common pattern: email to file?" → Email arrives → Apply to each attachment → Create file in OneDrive.

"Trigger fires twice (issue)?" → Use idempotency check or set concurrency control.

"Modify causes recursion?" → Add trigger condition to ignore the flow's own updates.

"VIP filter?" → Trigger condition using equals() expression.

"Get user details?" → Office 365 Users → Get user profile V2.

"Multiple flows on same trigger?" → Allowed; each independent.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Automated flows trigger on events from connected services without user intervention
  • Create via make.powerautomate.com → + Create → Automated cloud flow
  • Pick a connector trigger; common ones: Outlook (email), SharePoint (item), Teams (message), Forms (response)
  • Triggers have built-in filters (folder, sender, subject, etc.); use them to narrow events
  • Trigger conditions (advanced): expression-based filters before flow runs
  • Idiomatic patterns: email→file, item→notification, form→record, sync between systems
  • Apply to each loops over arrays (e.g., email attachments, list items)
  • Dynamic content references trigger and action outputs
  • Get-item-after-trigger is a common pattern to pull richer field set
  • Concurrency control: ... menu → Settings → parallel vs sequential
  • Idempotency: check audit log to prevent duplicate processing on retries
  • Avoid recursive triggers (flow modifies same item that triggers it)
  • Trigger conditions use expressions like @equals, @greater, @and, @contains
  • Use trigger conditions to filter before flow consumes request quota
  • Best practices: descriptive names, narrow triggers, error handling, idempotency, no hardcoded user data

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Instant flows are user-initiated — perfect when you want a button users press to start automation. They power "do this now" buttons in Power Apps, Teams, and SharePoint. The PL-100 exam tests instant flow triggers and Power Apps integration.

What instant flows are

Instant flow = cloud flow started by user action
 User clicks button → flow runs immediately
 Distinct from automated (event-driven) and scheduled (time-driven)

Trigger types:
 - "Manually trigger a flow" (Run from Power Automate)
 - "For a selected item / file / row" (SharePoint, Excel context)
 - "Power Apps (V2)" (Power Apps button)
 - "Microsoft Teams" instant trigger (Teams shortcut)

When to use:
 - User wants to "do this now" with explicit click
 - Manual checks before automation runs
 - Replace tedious manual steps
 - Power Apps backend logic
 - Approval requests

Distinct from automated:
 Automated: service detects event → flow auto-runs
 Instant: user explicitly triggers

"Manually trigger a flow"

Simplest instant trigger
Available everywhere: Power Automate portal, mobile app, Power Apps

Setup:
 + Create → Instant cloud flow
 Trigger: "Manually trigger a flow"
 Click Create

Trigger configuration:
 Add inputs (optional):
 Type: Text, Number, Boolean, Date, File, Email
 Description: hint shown when user runs
 Default value (optional)
 Mark required

User experience:
 Power Automate portal → My flows → "Run" button
 Mobile app → tap flow → fill inputs → run
 Power Apps button → trigger this flow

Inputs available downstream as dynamic content
 Reference like: trigger().outputs['inputs']['Text']

"For a selected item / file / row"

Context-specific instant trigger

Best practices for instant flows

★ PRACTICES
  • Use PowerApps V2 trigger over V1 — strongly typed, modern
  • Always respond to PowerApps at end (return success/message) for feedback
  • Avoid long-running flows for Power Apps callers; consider async pattern
  • Test in isolation first via Power Automate portal
  • Add error handling with Try-Catch (Scope action + Run After)
  • Don't pass sensitive data in flow inputs without encryption
  • Validate inputs at start of flow
  • Document inputs with clear descriptions
  • Version your flow — duplicate before major changes
  • Use environment variables for config that varies (URLs, IDs)

Common instant flow mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Mixing instant + automated on same trigger event — confusing
  2. No Respond to PowerApps action — caller hangs waiting
  3. Async assumed but flow runs synchronously — user waits
  4. Too many parameters — UX suffers
  5. Required field omitted — flow fails on missing input
  6. Power Apps formula calls flow on every recalc — wasted runs
  7. Flow needs admin permissions users don't have
  8. No timeout on long-running approval — flow stuck forever
  9. Sharing flow without considering connections — users prompted to re-auth
  10. Forget to Save before testing — runs old version
★ ON THE EXAM

"User-triggered flow type?" → Instant cloud flow.

"Trigger options for instant?" → Manually trigger, For selected item/file/row, Power Apps V2, Teams.

"Power Apps to flow integration?" → PowerApps V2 trigger.

"Return value from flow to Power Apps?" → "Respond to a PowerApp or flow" action.

"Inputs to instant flow?" → Define in trigger; Text/Number/Boolean/Date/File/Email types.

"Right-click in SharePoint?" → "For a selected item" trigger.

"Excel Online flow?" → "For a selected row" trigger; runs from Automate menu.

"Teams shortcut from message?" → "For a selected message" trigger.

"Call flow from Power Apps?" → button OnSelect: FlowName.Run(input1, input2).

"Old vs V2 trigger?" → V2 has strongly typed inputs and modern UX.

"Run instant flow?" → Power Automate portal / mobile / Power Apps button.

"Long-running flow from Power Apps?" → Async pattern; flow returns immediately, processes in background.

"User feedback?" → Notify in Power Apps based on flow response.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Instant flows are user-triggered: button clicks start them
  • Trigger types: Manually trigger a flow, For selected item/file/row, Power Apps V2, Teams
  • "Manually trigger" is simplest; runs from Power Automate portal/mobile
  • "For a selected item/file/row" provides context-specific triggers in SharePoint/Excel/OneDrive
  • "Power Apps V2" trigger enables flows to be called from Power Apps with typed inputs/outputs
  • Define inputs on instant triggers: Text, Number, Boolean, Date, File, Email
  • "Respond to a PowerApp or flow" action returns outputs to the caller
  • Power Apps integration: button OnSelect = FlowName.Run(inputs) → access outputs in variable
  • Common pattern: Power Apps form → instant flow → backend orchestration → return feedback
  • Teams instant flows enable right-click context actions on messages
  • Combine instant trigger with approval action for "submit for approval" workflows
  • Best practices: Use V2 triggers, always respond, validate inputs, error handling, environment vars
  • Don't put long-running operations in synchronous flows (UI waits)
  • Test instant flows in isolation (Power Automate "Run" button) before Power Apps integration
  • Multiple users can share an instant flow; each authenticates with own connection

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Scheduled flows run on a calendar — daily reports, weekly cleanups, hourly syncs. They're the third major flow type and essential for batch operations. The PL-100 exam tests recurrence configuration and common scheduled patterns.

What scheduled flows are

Scheduled cloud flow = runs on a calendar / clock-based trigger

Trigger: "Recurrence"
 Defines when and how often the flow runs

Examples:
 - Every day at 9am
 - Every Monday morning
 - Every 30 minutes during business hours
 - First day of each month
 - Every hour, on the hour

Distinct from automated (event-driven) and instant (user-driven)
 Scheduled runs without external trigger; just based on time

Use cases:
 - Daily summary reports
 - Weekly data cleanup
 - Periodic sync between systems
 - Reminder notifications
 - Polling APIs that don't have webhook triggers
 - Backup operations
 - Report generation

Creating a scheduled flow

make.powerautomate.com → + Create → Scheduled cloud flow

Initial setup:
 Name your flow
 Starting time: when first run should be
 Repeat every: interval (e.g., 1 Day)
 Click Create

Editor opens with Recurrence trigger configured
Add actions below

Recurrence trigger configuration

Recurrence trigger options:

Required:
 Interval — number (1, 2, 5, etc.)
 Frequency — Second / Minute / Hour / Day / Week / Month

Advanced:
 Time zone — specify TZ for date calculations
 Start time — when first run should occur
 
 On these days (for Week frequency):
 Sun / Mon / Tue / Wed / Thu / Fri / Sat
 Multi-select for "run on these days"
 
 At these hours (for Day / Week frequency):
 0-23 hour markers
 Run at specific times (e.g., 9, 12, 17 = 9am, 12pm, 5pm)
 
 At these minutes:
 0-59 minute markers
 Run at specific minutes within selected hours
 
 Time zone offset:
 Helpful for global teams

Examples:

Daily at 9am UTC:
 Interval: 1
 Frequency: Day
 Time zone: UTC
 At these hours: 9
 At these minutes: 0

Every 30 minutes during business hours Mon-Fri:
 Interval: 30
 Frequency: Minute
 On these days: Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri
 At these hours: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17

Weekly on Mondays at 9am:
 Interval: 1
 Frequency: Week
 On these days: Mon
 At these hours: 9
 At these minutes: 0

Frequency limits

Minimum interval depends on license:

Microsoft 365 Power Automate (basic):
 Minimum 5 minutes typically
 Higher for some accounts

Power Automate per User:
 Minimum 1 minute

Power Automate per Flow / Premium:
 Down to 1 second possible (in some scenarios)

Maximum interval:
 500 days typical

Best practices:
 - Don't poll faster than necessary
 - Each scheduled run uses request quota
 - For events, prefer webhook triggers (instant, no polling)
 - For data sync without events, scheduled flow is the right fit

Time zone considerations

Always specify time zone in the Recurrence trigger
Otherwise it runs in UTC by default

Common scenarios:

Global team:
 Time zone: UTC
 Run nightly at midnight UTC
 All users see consistent timing

Local office:
 Time zone: Eastern Time (US & Canada)
 Run at 9am ET
 Daylight saving handled automatically

Multi-timezone:
 Build separate flows per time zone
 Or use a single flow that runs in UTC and includes logic for per-TZ scheduling

Date arithmetic in actions:
 formatDateTime(utcNow(), 'yyyy-MM-dd')
 But Local time needs:
 formatDateTime(convertFromUtc(utcNow(), 'Eastern Standard Time'), 'yyyy-MM-dd')

Common pitfall:
 Daylight saving transitions can shift schedules
 Test around DST changeovers

Common scheduled patterns

Pattern 1: Daily report

Trigger: Recurrence daily at 9am ET

Actions:
 1. Get items from data source (filter for yesterday's records)
 2. Build summary table (Create CSV table or HTML table)
 3. Send email with table
 4. Optional: post in Teams channel

Variations:
 - Conditional: only send if data exists
 - Multiple recipients (based on filtering)
 - Multiple data sources combined
 - Filter by user/group/region for personalized reports

Pattern 2: Cleanup job

Trigger: Recurrence weekly on Sunday at 2am

Actions:
 1. Get items where Status = "Archived" AND Modified < 90 days ago
 2. Apply to each:
 Delete item
 3. Log count to audit table
 4. Email admin with summary

Use case: keep data tidy, manage storage, comply with retention

Pattern 3: Reminder notifications

Trigger: Recurrence hourly during business hours

Actions:
 1. Get items where DueDate = today + 1 day AND Status = "Pending"
 2. Apply to each:
 Get owner info
 Send reminder email
 3. Update last reminder sent timestamp

Variations:
 - Escalation logic (email if 3 days overdue, manager if 5 days, etc.)
 - Multiple channels (Teams + email)
 - Custom message templates

Pattern 4: Data sync

Trigger: Recurrence every 15 minutes (during sync window)

Actions:
 1. Get modified records from source A (filter: Modified > last_sync_time)
 2. For each:
 Update or create in destination B
 3. Save sync timestamp

Use case: keep two systems in sync without webhooks
 Useful for legacy systems without push notifications
 Less frequent than webhooks but still functional

Common scheduled flow mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. UTC time when local intended — runs at wrong wall-clock time
  2. Polling too frequently — high cost; throttling
  3. No time zone specified — defaults to UTC; surprises users
  4. Multiple identical scheduled flows — duplicate work
  5. Forgetting weekends — daily runs include weekends; use "On these days" filter
  6. Hardcoded date arithmetic — fails for edge cases (month rollover, leap year)
  7. No empty-data check — empty report sent if nothing found
  8. Long-running scheduled flow — could overlap with next scheduled run
  9. Daylight saving issues — schedules shift twice yearly
  10. No catch-up logic — if missed, data sync gap
★ ON THE EXAM

"Time-based flow?" → Scheduled cloud flow.

"Trigger?" → Recurrence.

"Frequency options?" → Second / Minute / Hour / Day / Week / Month.

"Run only Monday?" → Frequency: Week, On these days: Mon.

"Run only 9am?" → Frequency: Day, At these hours: 9, At these minutes: 0.

"Avoid weekends?" → Use "On these days" filter; uncheck Sat/Sun.

"Time zone?" → Specify explicitly; defaults to UTC.

"Daylight saving?" → Automatic if TZ specified; can shift schedules.

"Minimum interval?" → Depends on license; 5 min basic, 1 min premium.

"See next runs?" → Flow detail page shows upcoming scheduled executions.

"Date math in actions?" → formatDateTime, addDays, subtractFromTime, startOfMonth.

"Previous month range?" → startOfMonth(addToTime(utcNow(), -1, 'Month')).

"Polling vs scheduled?" → Polling is an automated trigger; scheduled is calendar-based.

"Multi-recipient report?" → Build distribution list as env variable or table.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Scheduled cloud flows run on calendar / clock-based triggers
  • Trigger is "Recurrence" with frequency (Second/Minute/Hour/Day/Week/Month) and interval
  • Advanced options: time zone, days of week, hours, minutes
  • Specify time zone explicitly to avoid UTC confusion
  • Common patterns: daily reports, weekly cleanup, hourly sync, monthly summaries
  • Minimum interval depends on license (5 min basic, 1 min premium)
  • Use "On these days" to filter weekdays / specific days
  • Use "At these hours/minutes" for clock-specific times
  • Date arithmetic functions: startOfMonth, addDays, subtractFromTime, formatDateTime
  • Each scheduled run uses request quota; don't poll more often than needed
  • "Next runs" display in flow detail page confirms schedule is correct
  • Daylight saving automatic with proper TZ; can still shift run times
  • Always include empty-data handling (don't send blank reports)
  • Long-running flows could overlap with next scheduled run; consider concurrency control
  • Webhook triggers are better than scheduled if events are available; use scheduled only for time-based logic
📊 FIGURE — scheduling without cron syntax
🎯 EXAM TIP
The Power Automate Recurrence trigger gives you cron-like power without cron syntax — you pick the interval, frequency, time zone, days and times from the UI. The time zone field is the real gain: cron has no notion of one, which is where a surprising share of scheduling bugs come from.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Approvals are one of Power Automate's most powerful built-in features. They wait for human decisions, integrate with email and Teams, and resume the flow based on the response. The PL-100 exam tests approval types, responses, and integrating approvals into flows.

What approvals are

Approval = built-in step that PAUSES a flow until a person makes a decision

Use cases:
 - Expense approval (manager signs off on submission)
 - Document review (peer review before publish)
 - Leave request (HR approves time-off)
 - Purchase order (finance approves spend)
 - Onboarding (multi-person sign-off)
 - Content publishing (editor approves before going live)

Why approvals matter:
 Human steps are bottlenecks in many workflows
 Approvals make them trackable, auditable, with deadlines
 Integrate into email and Teams for easy responses

Built-in actions:
 - Start and wait for an approval
 - Start an approval (without waiting; for async)
 - Create an approval (low-level; for advanced)
 - Get approvals (query existing)

Approval types

TypeBehavior
Approve / Reject - First to respondMultiple approvers; first decides
Approve / Reject - Everyone must approveAll approvers must approve (any reject stops it)
Custom Responses - Wait for one responseCustom buttons (e.g., "Approve / Request More Info / Reject")
Custom Responses - Wait for all responsesAll approvers must respond with custom options

Creating an approval action

In flow editor → + New step → search "Approval"

Pick: "Start and wait for an approval"

Configuration:
 Approval type: (one of 4 listed above)
 
 Title: short summary (shown to approver)
 "Expense approval: " + Title
 
 Assigned to: email addresses (comma-separated for multi-approver)
 Can use dynamic content (e.g., Manager.email)
 Multiple emails for First-to-respond or All-must-approve
 
 Details: full context for approver
 Markdown supported
 Include: amount, requester, attachments, justification
 
 Item link: URL to source record (e.g., SharePoint item)
 Item link description: text label for link
 
 Request reassignment: yes/no (allow approver to delegate)
 Reassign to: backup approver (optional)
 
 Approver requesting more info: yes/no

After this action:
 Flow PAUSES indefinitely (until approval responds)
 Resume on response with outputs available

Approver experience

Approver gets:
 Email notification (in Outlook):
 Subject: Approval request
 Body: title + details + decision buttons
 Click "Approve" or "Reject" inline → flow continues
 
 Teams notification:
 Approval card in chat
 Buttons to decide
 Comments field for justification
 
 Power Automate mobile app:
 See pending approvals
 Approve / reject with comments

Decision options:
 Approve / Reject (default)
 Approve / Request More Info
 Custom responses based on approval type
 
Comments field:
 Always available
 Captures rationale

Multi-approver scenarios:
 First to respond: only first response counts
 Everyone must approve: each must individually decide
 System tracks each approver's response

Reading approval response

After "Start and wait for approval" completes, outputs available:

 outcome: "Approve" / "Reject" / custom response
 responses: array of all approvers' responses
 each response has: approver, response, comments, time
 startTime, endTime
 approvers: list of approver objects

In dynamic content:
 outcome
 responses[0].responder.displayName
 responses[0].responder.email
 responses[0].comments

In expressions:
 outputs('approval')?['outcome']
 
Common conditional logic:
 Condition: outcome equals "Approve"
 Then: 
 Update record status to Approved
 Send confirmation to requester
 Take action (process payment, etc.)
 Else: 
 Update record status to Rejected
 Send rejection notice with comments

Multi-step / sequential approvals

Common business need: multiple approval stages

Pattern 1: Sequential (single approver per step)
 
 Step 1: Manager approval
 Start and wait for approval → outcome
 If Reject, stop with notification
 
 Step 2: Director approval (only if Step 1 was Approve)
 Condition: previous outcome = "Approve"
 Then: Start and wait for approval → outcome
 If Reject, stop
 
 Step 3: Final approval (only if Step 2 was Approve)
 ...

Pattern 2: Threshold-based
 
 Decision tree based on amount:
 If amount < 1000:
 Start manager approval
 Else if amount < 10000:
 Start manager + director sequential
 Else:
 Start manager + director + CFO sequential
 
 Use Switch action or nested Conditions

Pattern 3: Parallel approvals
 
 Multiple parallel branches each with approval
 Flow continues when ALL complete
 Use "Parallel branch" feature

Pattern 4: Voting
 
 Use "Everyone must approve" type
 Tally responses
 Decide based on majority

Email approval responses

Approvers can respond directly from email
No need to open Power Automate

In the email:
 Buttons: [Approve] [Reject]
 Click → opens browser → confirmation page
 Approval recorded in Power Automate
 Flow continues immediately

Configurable:
 Email template (default looks like standard approval email)
 Some customization via "Create approval" advanced action

In Outlook:
 Actionable messages: approval buttons appear inline
 Cleaner than clicking through to web page
 Available with proper Outlook + Power Automate setup

Mobile:
 Power Automate mobile app
 Built-in approvals tab
 See all pending and decide on the go

Worked example — multi-stage approval

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Expense approval with escalation

Approval timeouts and reminders

Pending approvals don't have built-in deadlines
But you can add expectations:

Reminder pattern:
 Approval action with timeout (less common)
 Or: parallel scheduled flow that checks pending approvals
 Run daily; for approvals pending > X days, send reminder

Escalation pattern:
 Configure escalation hierarchy
 After N days, re-assign to backup approver
 Use Power Automate's Reassign action

Time-out behavior:
 Approvals stay pending indefinitely by default
 No auto-expiration
 Flow runs forever in "Running" state
 Best practice: monitor and clean up old approvals

Custom expiration:
 Use Do-Until with check on time
 Or: Compose timeout date; on expire, take action

Common approval mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Approver email hardcoded — breaks when person leaves
  2. No reminder for pending approvals — sit forever
  3. Multi-approver with First-to-respond when All-must-approve was needed
  4. Approval after expensive action — should be before
  5. No condition check on outcome — flow proceeds even on Reject
  6. Missing details in approval body — approver lacks context
  7. Multiple parallel approvals when sequential is the business need
  8. No fallback if approver is OOO — flow stalls
  9. Approval action without proper return type handling
  10. Hard-coded approval cards style in email — limited customization
★ ON THE EXAM

"Pause flow for human decision?" → Approval action.

"Common approval action?" → "Start and wait for an approval".

"Approval types?" → Approve/Reject (First-to-respond, Everyone-must-approve), Custom Responses.

"Approver responds via?" → Email (inline buttons), Teams card, Power Automate mobile.

"Decision result?" → outcome field (Approve/Reject/custom).

"Multi-step approval?" → Sequential pattern with Condition between approvals.

"Multi-approver consensus?" → "Everyone must approve" type.

"Multi-approver race?" → "First to respond" type.

"Comments from approver?" → responses[0].comments in dynamic content.

"Approval timeouts?" → Not built-in; use parallel scheduled flow for reminders.

"Custom buttons?" → Custom Responses approval type.

"Approver out of office?" → Configure reassignment or have backup logic.

"Pre-approval audit?" → Pattern: Add to log → approval → update log with outcome.

"Approval data in actions?" → Use dynamic content: outcome, responder, comments.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Approvals pause a flow until a person makes a decision
  • Built-in actions: "Start and wait for an approval", "Start an approval", "Create an approval"
  • Four approval types: Approve/Reject First-to-respond, Approve/Reject Everyone-must-approve, Custom Wait-one, Custom Wait-all
  • Configure: title, assigned to, details, item link, reassignment options
  • Approvers respond via email (inline buttons), Teams card, or mobile app
  • Outputs available after approval: outcome (Approve/Reject/custom), responses, comments
  • Sequential pattern: chain approval → condition → next approval based on outcome
  • Parallel pattern: use "Parallel branch" for multiple simultaneous approvals
  • Threshold-based: switch on amount, choose appropriate approver chain
  • Use Office 365 Users connector to dynamically find manager / approvers
  • No built-in timeout; pending approvals wait indefinitely (monitor manually or with scheduled cleanup flow)
  • Reassignment lets approver delegate to backup
  • Capture audit data: who approved, when, comments — useful for compliance
  • Always include sufficient details in approval body for context
  • Best practice: dynamic approver emails (Office 365 Users.manager), not hardcoded
  • Multi-stage approvals: each level can have different approvers and conditions

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Connectors are how Power Automate touches the outside world. They're the same tiered system as Power Apps — Standard (free with Microsoft 365) vs Premium (extra license). Understanding which to use saves cost and avoids licensing surprises. The PL-100 exam tests this distinction.

Connector recap

A connector = pre-built bridge between Power Automate and a service

Each connector provides:

 Custom (build your own for unsupported APIs)

Three tiers:

License contagion

⚠ LICENSE CONTAGION

If a flow uses ANY premium connector:

  • The flow becomes a "premium flow"
  • The flow owner (creator) needs a premium license
  • Other USERS who use the flow may or may not need premium (depends on context)
  • Best practice: split apps/flows so standard-only ones remain free

Power Automate Premium licenses:

  • Power Automate per User: ~$15/user/month; unlimited flows + premium connectors
  • Power Automate per Flow: ~$100/flow/month; one flow, unlimited users
  • Power Automate Premium: includes RPA, AI Builder, hosted machines

Common connector mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Using premium connector when standard works — needless license cost
  2. Forgetting license contagion — flow becomes premium silently
  3. Service account connection lost — flow fails when account changes
  4. OAuth re-auth needed — connection expired; user prompted
  5. Wrong connector version — V2 vs V3; legacy vs new
  6. HTTP action without auth — call fails
  7. Premium connector triggering basic flow — license issue
  8. Custom connector schema wrong — actions fail
  9. Mixed connectors not testing edge cases
  10. No fallback when connector down — single point of failure
★ ON THE EXAM

"Connector tiers?" → Standard (free with M365) and Premium (extra license).

"Standard examples?" → SharePoint, Outlook, Teams, OneDrive, Excel Online, Office 365 Users.

"Premium examples?" → Dataverse, SQL Server, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, Dynamics 365.

"License contagion?" → If any premium connector used, flow becomes premium.

"Per User vs Per Flow license?" → Per User: $15/user; Per Flow: $100/flow.

"On-premises SQL?" → Premium + On-premises Data Gateway.

"Custom connector?" → Wrap your own REST API via OpenAPI/Postman.

"HTTP action?" → Direct REST call; premium connector typically.

"Auth models?" → OAuth 2.0 (default), API Key, Basic, Anonymous, Windows, Service Principal.

"Connections per user or shared?" → Default per-user; shared possible via service account.

"Throttling on connectors?" → Yes; rate limits per service; HTTP 429 on exceed.

"AI Builder?" → Premium feature for AI-powered actions in flows.

"Connection list?" → Power Automate portal → Connections.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Connectors are pre-built bridges to services; same model as Power Apps
  • Three tiers: Standard (free with M365), Premium (extra license), Custom (your APIs)
  • Standard: Office 365 (Outlook, SharePoint, Teams, OneDrive, etc.), basic third-party
  • Premium: Dataverse, SQL Server, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, AI Builder, Dynamics 365
  • License contagion: ANY premium connector → entire flow requires premium
  • Power Automate per User (~$15) or per Flow (~$100) licenses for premium
  • On-premises connectors require On-premises Data Gateway
  • HTTP action allows direct REST API calls (typically premium)
  • Custom connectors wrap your APIs via OpenAPI/Postman specs
  • Auth models: OAuth 2.0 (most), API Key, Basic, Anonymous, Windows, Service Principal
  • Connections are per-user by default; service accounts for production
  • Common standard triggers: email, item, message, file created/modified events
  • Common standard actions: get items, send email, post message, create file
  • 1000+ connectors available; Microsoft + third-party partners build them
  • Each connector has its own rate limits; HTTP 429 on throttle
  • Mix standard + premium thoughtfully to manage license costs

 - Handle missing fields (some users lack manager, etc.)
 - Premium-equivalent operations require User.Read.All in some contexts

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS

  9. Adaptive card JSON malformed — Teams rejects
  10. Old V1/V2 actions when V3+ available — missing features

  • Microsoft 365 connectors are standard tier; included with M365 license
  • Most-used: Outlook, SharePoint, Teams, OneDrive, Excel Online, Office 365 Users, Forms, Planner

  • SharePoint: list items and files; CRUD operations; triggers on create/modify
  • Teams: post messages, create channels, adaptive cards; triggers on messages and mentions

  • Standard connectors cover most M365 automation needs; no premium license required

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

When no built-in connector exists for the service you need, custom connectors are the answer. They wrap any REST API so you can use it like a first-class connector across all your flows and apps. The PL-100 exam tests recognizing when to use custom connectors.

What custom connectors are

Custom connector = your wrapper around a REST API
 Makes any service available to Power Automate (and Power Apps)
 Treated as first-class connector in flows

Why custom connectors:
 - Use any REST API in your flows
 - Internal company APIs (not in catalog)
 - Third-party APIs without built-in connectors
 - Wrap legacy systems with REST shims
 - Centralize API logic for reuse

What you provide:
 - API definition (OpenAPI/Swagger or Postman collection)
 - Authentication method
 - Test data for verification

What Power Automate provides:
 - Drag-and-drop usage in flows
 - Built-in authentication handling
 - Dynamic content recognition
 - Available in Power Apps too

When to use custom connectors

ScenarioSolution
Calling Microsoft 365 serviceUse built-in standard connector
Calling Salesforce / SAP / ServiceNowUse built-in premium connector
Calling your company's internal APIBuild custom connector
Calling third-party SaaS not in catalogBuild custom connector
One-off REST callUse HTTP action (premium)
Public API with no authHTTP action or simple custom connector

Creating a custom connector

make.powerautomate.com → Custom Connectors → + New custom connector

Or in Solutions:
 Solutions → your solution → + New → Custom Connector

Two starting options:
 1. Create from blank (manual setup)
 2. Import an OpenAPI file (.yaml/.json with API definition)
 3. Import from URL (OpenAPI hosted)
 4. Import a Postman collection (.json)

Manual setup steps (5 tabs):

 Tab 1: General
 - Icon and color
 - Description
 - Scheme: HTTPS
 - Host: api.yourcompany.com (no protocol)
 - Base URL: /v1 (path prefix)
 
 Tab 2: Security
 - Auth type:
 No authentication
 API Key
 OAuth 2.0
 Basic auth
 Generic OAuth 2.0
 - Configure based on auth type
 
 Tab 3: Definition
 - Define operations (HTTP endpoints):
 Each = trigger or action
 Method: GET / POST / PUT / DELETE / PATCH
 URL path
 Request: parameters, headers, body schema
 Response: schema, sample data
 
 Tab 4: Code (optional)
 - C# or PowerShell scripts for advanced transformations
 - Pre-request and post-response logic
 - Useful: data shaping, custom auth
 
 Tab 5: Test
 - Create a connection
 - Test each operation with sample data
 - Verify response

After creation:
 Available in your environment
 Appears in connector search
 Use in flows/apps like any other connector

OpenAPI / Swagger

OpenAPI = standard for documenting REST APIs
 Formerly called Swagger
 YAML or JSON format
 Defines: endpoints, parameters, request/response schemas, auth

Example OpenAPI document fragment:

openapi: 3.0.0
info:
 title: My API
 version: 1.0.0
servers:
 - url: https://api.example.com/v1
paths:
 /customers:
 get:
 summary: List customers
 operationId: ListCustomers
 parameters:
 - name: limit
 in: query
 schema:
 type: integer
 responses:
 '200':
 description: OK
 content:
 application/json:
 schema:
 type: array
 items:
 $ref: '#/components/schemas/Customer'

When you import this:
 Power Automate auto-generates:
 Action: "List customers"
 Parameters: limit (number)
 Response: array of Customer objects
 
 Each Customer field becomes dynamic content

Documentation:
 Many APIs publish OpenAPI specs
 Tools: Swagger UI, ReDoc
 Generators: from code to OpenAPI

Postman collections

Postman = popular API testing tool

Postman collection = exported JSON of API requests
 Useful starting point for custom connectors

To convert:
 1. In Postman, organize requests into a collection
 2. Add test responses (helpful for schema)
 3. Export collection (right-click → Export → v2.1)
 4. Import into Power Automate custom connector

Power Automate generates:
 Each request → operation
 Parameters from request body
 Response schema from sample
 Authentication from Postman environment

Limitations:
 Not all Postman features map perfectly
 Some manual cleanup may be needed
 Test thoroughly before sharing

Authentication options

No authentication:
 Public APIs (rare for business use)
 Simple for prototypes

API Key:
 Most common for internal APIs
 Token in header or query param
 Configure: parameter name, location
 Each connection has its own key

OAuth 2.0:
 Standard for OAuth-compliant services
 Configure:
 Client ID, Client Secret
 Authorization URL
 Token URL
 Refresh URL
 Scope
 More complex setup; auto-handles refresh

Basic Auth:
 Username + password
 Sent base64-encoded in header
 Less secure; legacy systems

Generic OAuth 2.0:
 More flexible OAuth setup
 Custom auth flows
 Advanced scenarios

Windows authentication:
 For on-premises calls via gateway

Service account vs per-user:
 Per-user: each user creates own connection
 Service account: shared connection (advanced)

Custom connector lifecycle

Stages:

1. Local development:
 Created in your environment only
 Visible to you and shared users
 Test thoroughly

2. Share within environment:
 Co-owners can edit
 Users can create connections and use it
 Per-environment availability

3. Share with another environment:
 Export from source env
 Import to target env
 Package as part of solution

4. Certification (for partners):
 Submit to Microsoft for review
 Once approved, becomes globally available
 Listed in connector catalog for all Power Platform users
 Rare; typically for ISVs

Best practices:
 - Build connector in a solution for portability
 - Test in dev environment first
 - Document each operation
 - Version your API; update connector as API changes
 - Use environment variables for env-specific config

Using a custom connector in flows

After custom connector is created:

In a flow:
 + New step → Custom (tab) → search your connector
 Or in main search, look for the name

Connection setup:
 First use: prompt to create connection
 Provide credentials based on auth type
 Test connection
 Save

Use action:
 Same as built-in actions
 Parameters appear as form fields
 Outputs are dynamic content

Test:
 Run flow; verify connector calls succeed
 Check API response in run history

Common issues:
 - Wrong URL or endpoint
 - Auth credentials incorrect
 - Request body schema mismatched
 - Network/firewall blocks

Debugging:
 Custom connector definition Test tab
 Test individual operations there
 Use API documentation as reference

HTTP action alternative

For one-off REST calls, the HTTP action is simpler:

Action: HTTP (premium)
 Method: GET / POST / PUT / DELETE / PATCH
 URI: full URL
 Headers: dictionary
 Body: JSON or other
 Authentication: None / Basic / OAuth / Managed Service Identity
 
 Response:
 statusCode, headers, body
 Body parseable as JSON via Parse JSON action

When to use HTTP action vs custom connector:
 HTTP action:
 Quick one-off call
 Not reused across flows
 Don't want to maintain a connector
 
 Custom connector:
 Same API used in multiple flows
 Want centralized logic
 Want type-safe parameters
 Want easy sharing with other makers

HTTP action is premium (in most plans)
Custom connector premium-equivalent depends on wrapped API

Common custom connector mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. OpenAPI spec wrong or outdated — connector doesn't match API
  2. Auth misconfigured — all calls fail with 401
  3. Schema mismatch — request body fields wrong → 400 errors
  4. Hardcoded URLs — different per environment; use env variables
  5. No error handling in flow when connector fails
  6. Forgetting to share connector — co-makers can't use it
  7. Auth token expiration not handled — flow fails after refresh time
  8. Test only the happy path — production errors surprise you
  9. Sharing connector but not credentials — users can't connect
  10. Versioning ignored — old connector breaks when API updates
★ ON THE EXAM

"Connect to internal API?" → Custom connector.

"Wrap REST API as connector?" → Custom connector.

"Import API definition?" → OpenAPI / Swagger or Postman collection.

"Create from existing API spec?" → Import OpenAPI YAML/JSON.

"Auth options?" → No auth, API Key, OAuth 2.0, Basic auth, Generic OAuth 2.0, Windows.

"One-off HTTP call?" → HTTP action (premium).

"Reusable across flows?" → Custom connector.

"Custom connector lifecycle?" → Local → environment-shared → multi-env solution → certified.

"OpenAPI vs Swagger?" → Same thing; OpenAPI is newer name.

"Where created?" → Power Automate → Custom Connectors.

"Available to?" → Same environment users by default; shareable.

"Use in Power Apps too?" → Yes; same connector available.

"License?" → Tier depends on what the wrapped API is; check your scenario.

"Test operations?" → In connector's Test tab during build.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Custom connectors wrap any REST API to make it usable in Power Automate (and Power Apps)
  • Build via Power Automate → Custom Connectors → + New custom connector
  • Three starting points: blank manual setup, OpenAPI import, Postman collection import
  • OpenAPI (formerly Swagger) is the standard for documenting REST APIs (YAML or JSON)
  • Configure: General (URLs, icon), Security (auth), Definition (operations), Code (optional), Test
  • Auth options: No auth, API Key, OAuth 2.0, Basic, Generic OAuth, Windows
  • Each operation = trigger or action in flows
  • Available in same environment; shareable to other envs via solutions
  • Can submit for certification to become globally available (rare; ISVs)
  • HTTP action (premium) is simpler for one-off REST calls
  • Use custom connector when API is reused across flows; HTTP action for one-off
  • Build in solutions for portability between environments
  • Test in connector's Test tab before using in flows
  • Document each operation; provide example data
  • Auth credentials per-user by default; service accounts for production
  • Watch API versioning; update custom connector when API changes
