◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Dynamic content is how a flow's actions consume the outputs of earlier steps — trigger data, action results, variables. Without it, every flow would be a series of hardcoded steps. Understanding tokens vs expressions is critical for PL-100.

What dynamic content is

Dynamic content = values from previous steps available to current step

How it appears:
 Click in any input field of an action
 Right-side panel slides open with "Dynamic content" tab
 Lists all outputs from earlier steps
 Click any item → inserts as a "token" pill in the field

Tokens vs raw text:
 When inserted, the token shows as a colored chip with the field name
 At runtime, Power Automate substitutes the actual value
 You can mix tokens and typed text

Two tabs in the side panel:
 Dynamic content — pre-built tokens for outputs
 Expression — write a function call

Where outputs come from

Trigger outputs:
 Every trigger emits data
 For "When email arrives": From, To, Subject, Body, Attachments, etc.
 For "When item created": ID, Title, all column values
 For "Recurrence": current time

Action outputs:
 Every action emits data after it runs
 "Get item" → all the item's columns
 "Send email" → status, message ID
 "Compose" → whatever you composed
 "Initialize variable" → variable name (used in expressions)

Variable values:
 After Initialize/Set variable → the variable's current value
 Accessed via dynamic content under the variable name

Available scope:
 An action can use outputs from ANY earlier step
 Cannot use outputs from later steps (logical)
 Inside Apply to each, "current item" of the loop is available

Token examples

Example flow: email arrives → save attachments → notify

Step 1: When new email arrives (trigger)
 Output tokens available:
 From, To, Subject, Body
 Has Attachment, Importance
 Received Time, Message ID
 Attachments (array)

Step 2: Apply to each attachment
 Output tokens (within loop):
 Attachment Content (binary)
 Attachment Name (string)
 Attachment Content Type

Step 3: Create file in OneDrive
 Inputs need:
 Folder Path: type "/Email Attachments/" (no token; static)
 File Name: insert token → Attachment Name
 File Content: insert token → Attachment Content
 
 These appear as colored pills in the input fields

Step 4: Send notification email
 Inputs need:
 To: type "team@example.com" (or use trigger From for reply-to-sender pattern)
 Subject: type "Attachment received: " + insert Attachment Name
 Body: HTML with mixed tokens
 "Received an email from " + From + " with attachment " + Attachment Name + "."

Inserting tokens

Method 1: Click in field → side panel → click token
 Most common
 Auto-suggests relevant tokens
 Search box at top to find by name

Method 2: Type "@" in field → autocomplete suggests
 Older interface
 Faster for power users

Method 3: Drag from side panel
 Some browsers support drag-and-drop

After insert:
 Token appears as colored pill (often blue or purple)
 Click pill to see token details (path + value)
 Delete pill: backspace from end of field

Tokens are not pure strings:
 Internally, Power Automate stores them as references
 At runtime, the reference resolves to the actual value
 Mixing tokens with typed text auto-concatenates

Mixing tokens and text

In a single field, you can mix:
 Static typed text
 Multiple tokens
 Expression-based values (see next section)

Example email body:
 "Hi {{User Name}},
 
 Your order {{Order ID}} has been processed.
 
 Total: ${{Order Total}}
 Status: {{Status}}
 
 Thank you,
 Team"

Where {{...}} represents inserted tokens. Static text in between.

Result at runtime:
 "Hi Sarah Johnson,
 
 Your order ORD-12345 has been processed.
 
 Total: $129.99
 Status: Shipped
 
 Thank you,
 Team"

Power Automate handles the concatenation automatically.

Token paths and outputs() syntax

When you insert a token, Power Automate generates an expression
 Visible in the underlying JSON definition of the flow

For trigger outputs:
 triggerOutputs()?['body/Subject']
 triggerOutputs()?['body/From']
 triggerOutputs()?['headers/Importance']

For action outputs:
 outputs('ActionName')?['body/PropertyName']
 body('ActionName')?['PropertyName']
 
 Note: outputs() returns whole output object; body() returns just body

For variables:
 variables('VariableName')

The ? (question mark) is a null-safe accessor:
 ?['x'] → if path is null, returns null instead of error
 Safer for optional fields

Use these in:
 Expression tab of dynamic content
 Trigger conditions
 Calculated field values
 Anywhere you need an expression

Apply to each: ThisItem

When you wrap actions in Apply to each:
 Loops over an array
 Each iteration has the "current item"

Reference the current item:
 Dynamic content shows the array's element schema
 E.g., for SharePoint items: ID, Title, columns
 E.g., for attachments: Name, Content

In expressions:
 items('Apply_to_each')?['fieldName']
 
 Or for nested loops:
 items('Apply_to_each_2')?['fieldName']

You can:
 Reference outer scope's variables (from before loop)
 Reference trigger outputs (always available)
 Reference outputs of actions inside the loop (for subsequent actions)

But you CANNOT:
 Reference outputs from outside the loop that came AFTER the loop started
 Reference current item of OTHER loops (use loop-specific items() with name)

JSON property access

Many connector outputs are complex JSON
Dynamic content shows top-level fields automatically

For nested properties:
 "Get item" might return:
 {
 ID: 5,
 Title: "Sample",
 Author: {
 Email: "user@example.com",
 DisplayName: "User Name"
 },
 Tags: ["red", "blue"]
 }

Access nested:
 Top-level: dynamic content → ID, Title, Author, Tags
 Author.Email: 
 Expression: outputs('Get_item')?['body/Author/Email']
 Or: nested in dynamic content tree

Parse JSON action:
 If you receive raw JSON string:
 Compose action with the JSON
 Parse JSON action: input + schema (paste sample to auto-generate)
 Then properties available as dynamic content

For arrays:
 Access first item: first(array)
 Access last: last(array)
 Index: array?[0], array?[1]
 Filter, map, transform — use array functions

Most useful expressions for paths:
 outputs('Step_Name')
 body('Step_Name')
 triggerOutputs()
 variables('Name')
 items('Apply_to_each')
 iterationIndexes('Apply_to_each')

Compose action — staging values

Compose = simple action that stores a value for later use

When to use:
 - Test/preview an expression result
 - Stash intermediate calculations
 - Build complex strings step-by-step
 - Create dummy data for testing

Usage:
 + Add action → Compose
 Inputs: anything (expression, dynamic content, JSON, etc.)
 
 Output: the value you composed
 Available downstream as dynamic content

Example:
 Compose: addDays(utcNow(), -7)
 Stores "7 days ago" as a usable value
 
 Compose JSON:
 { "name": triggerOutputs()?['body/Name'], "amount": variables('Total') }
 Creates object for downstream use
 
 Compose with concat:
 concat('Hi ', triggerOutputs()?['body/From'], ', your order...')
 Builds string template

Best practices:
 - Use Compose when you'll reference the value multiple times (saves expression complexity)
 - Compose to test an expression's output (preview by running)
 - Avoid: chains of Composes when a single one would do

Empty / missing field handling

Optional fields may be missing or null

Without handling:
 Token returns null → action may fail
 Especially: Send email needs body text; null causes error

With handling (use expressions):
 
 coalesce: return first non-null
 coalesce(triggerOutputs()?['body/Optional'], 'default value')
 
 if + empty: check before using
 if(empty(triggerOutputs()?['body/X']), 'default', triggerOutputs()?['body/X'])
 
 Null check:
 if(equals(triggerOutputs()?['body/X'], null), 'default', triggerOutputs()?['body/X'])

For arrays:
 Empty array: empty(array) → true
 Array with nulls: filter to non-null before using

Production tip:
 Always handle missing fields defensively
 Especially for: optional inputs, user-supplied data, external API responses

Outputs vs Body vs Result

Three ways to reference action outputs:

outputs('ActionName')
 Returns the FULL output object: { headers, body, statusCode }
 Use when you need headers, status, or full structure

body('ActionName')
 Returns just the body property of the output
 Same as outputs('ActionName')?['body']
 Most common; what you want 90% of the time

outputs('ActionName')?['body/property']
 Combined: outputs + body access + property
 Quick path for specific value

Examples:
 Send Email V2 output:
 outputs('Send_email_V2') → full response
 body('Send_email_V2') → { id, etc. } (the message ID etc.)
 outputs('Send_email_V2')?['body/id'] → just the ID

For Get items (returns array):
 body('Get_items')?['value'] → the array of items
 Use Apply to each on the array

Common dynamic content mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Hardcoded values where tokens would work — inflexible flow
  2. Missing null checks — flow fails on empty optional fields
  3. Wrong action name in expression — typo → null result
  4. Using outputs() when body() needed (or vice versa)
  5. Tokens inside Apply to each from outside loop — out of scope error
  6. Forgetting Parse JSON when working with raw JSON strings
  7. Array vs object confusion — accessing as if scalar when actually array
  8. Token field renamed — flow breaks (action output schema changed)
  9. Compose chains instead of single expression — wasteful
  10. Long flow with many tokens hard to debug — consider variables for clarity
★ ON THE EXAM

"Output of previous steps?" → Dynamic content.

"Insert?" → Click input field; side panel; click token.

"@ symbol?" → Type @ in field to invoke dynamic content (older interface).

"triggerOutputs()?" → Function returning trigger's output object.

"outputs('X')?" → Action X's full output object.

"body('X')?" → Action X's body property only.

"?[x] vs [x]?" → ?[x] is null-safe; [x] errors on null path.

"Compose action?" → Stage a value for later use.

"Variable in expression?" → variables('Name').

"Loop current item?" → items('Apply_to_each').

"Mixed tokens and text?" → Yes; same field can have both.

"Null-safe handling?" → coalesce, if + empty, ? operator.

"Parse JSON?" → Action that takes JSON string + schema; emits typed dynamic content.

"Get array from action returning JSON?" → body('Action')?['value'] commonly.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Dynamic content = outputs from previous steps available to current action
  • Insert tokens via right side panel (click in input field) or type @
  • Tokens appear as colored chips; can mix with static text
  • Sources: trigger outputs, action outputs, variables
  • Internal syntax: triggerOutputs(), outputs('Name'), body('Name'), variables('Name')
  • Null-safe accessor ? in paths: ?['field'] returns null instead of error
  • outputs() returns full object; body() returns just body property
  • Inside Apply to each, items('LoopName') accesses current iteration item
  • Compose action stages a value for later reuse (testing or reuse)
  • Parse JSON action converts raw JSON strings to dynamic content
  • Handle missing fields with coalesce, if+empty, or null checks
  • Action names in expressions use underscores ('Send_an_email' for "Send an email")
  • Renaming actions breaks downstream expressions — careful with action renames
  • Mixing too many inline tokens makes flows hard to debug; consider variables
  • Schema changes in connectors can break flows that use specific token paths

Expression debugging

When an expression fails:

1. Check expression syntax:
 - Missing parentheses
 - Misspelled function name
 - Wrong number of parameters

2. Check field paths:
 - body/Name vs body/name (case-sensitive)
 - Use ?[] for null-safe (avoids errors)
 - Verify in Run history what the actual output looks like

3. Test in Compose first:
 - Add Compose action with your expression
 - Run flow → see Compose output
 - Iterate until correct

4. Use formatDateTime() for dates:
 - Don't try to manipulate date strings directly
 - Always go through Date type

5. String types:
 - Convert numbers with string() before concat
 - concat won't auto-convert

6. Null handling:
 - Use coalesce or if(empty, ...) for safety

Common errors:
 "InvalidTemplate" - syntax wrong
 "Property does not exist" - typo in field path
 "Cannot convert" - type mismatch (string vs number)
 "Out of range" - substring/index past length

  5. Wrong date format string — use yyyy-MM-dd format
  6. String comparison case-sensitive — use toLower() for both sides
  7. Substring out of range — check length first
  8. Forgetting time zone — utcNow() returns UTC
  9. Hardcoded ticks per day — use addDays/subtractFromTime instead
  10. Treating null as empty string — they're different (use coalesce)

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Real flows branch — "if email contains 'urgent' then escalate, else file in archive." Power Automate gives you two branching actions: Condition (two-way) and Switch (multi-way). Knowing when to use which keeps flows readable instead of nested-if-stair monsters.

The Condition action

Condition action (Control > Condition):
 Evaluates ONE comparison (or compound) → splits into 2 branches
 
 Layout:
 [Trigger]
 [Condition: Status == "Active"]
 ├─ If yes
 │ [Actions for yes branch]
 └─ If no
 [Actions for no branch]

Builder fields:
 Choose a value: (left side — usually a dynamic content token)
 Operator: (is equal to, contains, etc.)
 Choose a value: (right side — constant or token)

After condition runs:
 Only ONE branch executes
 Other branch is skipped (status = "Skipped")
 Flow continues after the condition block

You can leave either branch EMPTY:
 If no actions, branch is just skipped silently

Operators in conditions

OperatorUse case
is equal toExact match (text, numbers, booleans)
is not equal toAnything except this value
is greater than / less thanNumeric comparison
is greater/less than or equal toInclusive numeric comparison
containsSubstring search in text
does not containSubstring not present
starts with / ends withAnchor-based text match
is empty / is not emptyNull/blank check

Compound conditions (AND / OR)

In the Condition action, click "+ Add" → "Add row" or "Add group"

Row: single comparison
Group: nested condition (for parenthesization)

AND/OR toggle at top of each group

Example — escalate if (Status = "Open" AND Priority = "High"):
 Condition
 Status is equal to "Open"
 AND
 Priority is equal to "High"

Example — notify if (Status = "Failed" OR Status = "Error"):
 Condition
 Status is equal to "Failed"
 OR
 Status is equal to "Error"

Example — nested logic:
 (Status = "Open" AND Priority = "High") OR Customer = "VIP"
 
 Top-level OR
 Group 1 (AND)
 Status = "Open"
 Priority = "High"
 Group 2 (single)
 Customer = "VIP"

Expression-based conditions (advanced mode)

If the visual builder doesn't express what you need, switch to advanced mode (click the icon next to the operator). Enter an expression that evaluates to true or false:

@equals(triggerBody()?['Status'], 'Open')

@greater(int(triggerBody()?['Age']), 18)

@and(
 equals(triggerBody()?['Status'], 'Open'),
 greater(int(triggerBody()?['Priority']), 5)
)

@or(
 contains(triggerBody()?['Subject'], 'urgent'),
 contains(triggerBody()?['Subject'], 'critical')
)

@not(empty(triggerBody()?['Description']))

@startsWith(triggerBody()?['Email'], 'admin')

# Date comparisons (use ticks() for safe comparison):
@greater(ticks(triggerBody()?['DueDate']), ticks(utcNow()))

# When advanced mode is the only option:
- Comparing dates
- Checking if a value is NULL vs empty string
- Complex string parsing
- Calling functions like length() or json()

Common condition pitfalls

⚠ COMMON GOTCHAS
  1. Comparing number-strings as numbers — "10" > "9" returns FALSE because string compare. Wrap with int() or float().
  2. Boolean as text "true" — Some sources return booleans as strings. Use @equals(string(value), 'true').
  3. Empty vs null — "is empty" catches both empty string AND null. Use @equals(value, null) for null-only check.
  4. Case sensitivity — "contains" is case-sensitive. Use @contains(toLower(text), 'urgent') for case-insensitive.
  5. Choice fields in SharePoint — Single-select Choice column returns {Value: 'x'} object, not just 'x'. Use triggerBody()?['Status']?['Value'].
  6. Date in wrong format — String compare on dates breaks across months. Convert with ticks() first.
  7. Person field comparisons — Person fields are objects: {DisplayName, Email, ...}. Compare specific subfield.
  8. Approval responses — "Approve" vs "Reject" — exact case matters; use the dynamic content token, don't type it.

The Switch action

Switch action (Control > Switch):
 Evaluates ONE value → matches it against multiple cases
 Cleaner than nested Conditions for multi-way branching
 
 Layout:
 Switch on: Status
 ├─ Case: "Open" → [actions]
 ├─ Case: "Pending" → [actions]
 ├─ Case: "Closed" → [actions]
 └─ Default → [actions for anything else]

When to use Switch:
 - One value, many possible matches
 - Each case has different actions
 - Replaces nested if/elif/elif/else chains

When NOT to use Switch:
 - Need ranges (use Condition with > and <)
 - Need compound logic (Status = X AND Priority = Y)
 - Only two outcomes (Condition is simpler)

Switch — building it

1. Insert Switch action
2. "On" field: dynamic content (e.g., triggerOutputs > Status)
3. Each case has:
 Equals: value to match (string, number)
 Inside: actions for this case
4. "+ Add case" for each new branch
5. "Default" case runs if NO case matched
 (Optional — empty default = silently pass through)

Important:
 - Switch ONLY supports EQUALS comparison
 - One value per case (no ranges, no patterns)
 - Case sensitivity follows the data source
 - Can have many cases; flow editor scrolls

Performance:
 Switch is faster than nested Conditions
 All cases visible at once → easier to read

▣ EXAMPLE: Route support emails

Scenario: Incoming email's Subject prefix determines which team to notify.

Trigger: When a new email arrives (V3)

Action: Initialize variable
 Name: prefix
 Type: String

Action: Switch

 Case: '[BILLING]'

Worked example — Condition with compound logic

▣ EXAMPLE: SLA escalation

Scenario: Escalate tickets that are HIGH priority AND older than 24 hours AND still open.

Trigger: Recurrence (every hour)

Action: List rows present in a table (Dataverse)
 Table: Tickets
 Filter: statuscode eq 'Open'

Action: Apply to each (ticket from list)
 
 Action: Condition (AND group)
 Row 1: priority is equal to "High"
 Row 2: createdon is less than @addHours(utcNow(), -24)
 
 If yes:
 Action: Send email
 To: oncall-manager@company.com
 Subject: SLA breach risk: @{item()?['title']}
 Body: This ticket has been open >24h at High priority.
 
 Action: Update row (Dataverse)
 Set escalated = Yes
 
 If no:
 (empty branch — no action)

Could also write this entirely as an OData filter on the List rows action to reduce inner branching.

Choosing Condition vs Switch vs filter-at-source

SituationUse
Two outcomes (yes/no, true/false)Condition
One value, 3+ possible matchesSwitch
Range checks (age > 18 AND age < 65)Condition (compound)
Different criteria per branchCondition with nested branches
Filter to specific subset before processingOData filter on list action (most efficient)
Multiple unrelated checksSequential Conditions (early-exit pattern)

Early exit pattern with Terminate

For input validation, exit flow early if precondition fails:

Trigger: When item is created

Action: Condition — Status field is empty
 If yes:
 Action: Terminate
 Status: Failed
 Code: InvalidInput
 Message: "Status field is required"
 If no:
 (proceed with rest of flow)

Action: Condition — Priority is empty
 If yes:
 Action: Terminate (same pattern)
 If no:
 (continue)

Result: clean validation gate at top of flow
Avoid: deeply nesting all logic inside the "If no" branch

Configure run-after for skipped branches

By default, an action runs only if its predecessor SUCCEEDED.

Sometimes you want an action to run after EITHER branch of a condition:

 Condition
 If yes: Action A
 If no: Action B
 ↓
 Action C

Want C to run after A succeeds OR after B succeeds:
 
 Configure run-after on Action C:
 Right-click → "Configure run after"
 Check: "has succeeded" AND "has failed" AND "is skipped"
 
 Now C runs no matter which branch executed

Common use:
 Final notification or cleanup that should always happen
★ ON THE EXAM

"Two-way branch?" → Condition.

"Multi-way branch on one value?" → Switch.

"Range or compound logic?" → Condition (Switch only does equals).

"Combine AND/OR?" → Condition with groups.

"Exit flow early?" → Terminate action.

"Run after either branch?" → Configure run-after.

"Default in Switch?" → Catches unmatched values; optional.

"Comparing numbers stored as strings?" → Convert with int() or float().

"Case-insensitive contains?" → Advanced mode: @contains(toLower(x), 'y').

"SharePoint Choice field?" → Object — use .Value subfield.

  • Condition action = two branches (if yes / if no) on a comparison
  • Switch action = many branches on equality to a single value
  • Switch only supports EQUALS; Condition supports many operators
  • Use Condition for ranges, compound logic, two outcomes
  • Use Switch for clean multi-way matching on one variable
  • Compound conditions use AND/OR with Add row and Add group
  • Advanced mode lets you write expressions for non-standard logic
  • Watch for type issues: strings comparing as text not numbers; booleans as "true" strings
  • SharePoint Choice/Person fields are objects — drill into subfields
  • Use Terminate for early exit on validation failure
  • Configure run-after to merge branches back together
  • Empty branches are valid (silently skipped)
  • Filtering at the source (OData $filter) is more efficient than filtering with Condition after
  • Avoid deeply nested Conditions — use Switch or filter-first pattern

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Real automation processes lots of things at once — "for every new file in this folder, send a confirmation," "for each row in a CSV, create a record." Power Automate has two loop actions: Apply to each (iterate a known array) and Do until (iterate while a condition is true). These are the workhorses of bulk processing.

The Apply to each action

Apply to each (Control > Apply to each):
 Iterates over an ARRAY (collection)
 Runs the inner actions ONCE per element

Inputs:
 Any array — from a List action, parsed JSON, split string, etc.
 
 Examples:
 - List rows present in table → returns array of rows
 - Get items (SharePoint) → returns array of items 
 - Get attachments → returns array of attachments
 - split('a,b,c', ',') → returns ['a','b','c']

Auto-insertion:
 When you pick a dynamic content token INSIDE an array,
 Power Automate auto-wraps the action in Apply to each.

Accessing the current item

Inside Apply to each, the current element is item():

 item() — the whole element
 item()?['Title'] — Title property
 item()?['Author']?['Email'] — nested property
 item()['Status'] — same as ?['Status'] (no null check)

Dynamic content panel:
 Shows the array's properties as tokens
 Picking one inserts item()?['propertyName']

For nested loops:
 items('outer_loop_name') — refers to outer loop's current item
 items('inner_loop_name') — refers to inner loop's current item
 item() alone refers to innermost loop by default

Apply to each — concurrency

By default, Apply to each runs iterations in PARALLEL:
 - Default concurrency: 20 parallel iterations
 - Max: 50

Configure:
 Click "..." on Apply to each → Settings
 Concurrency Control: On
 Degree of Parallelism: 1 to 50

When to set Concurrency = 1 (sequential):
 - Order matters (writing log entries chronologically)
 - Modifying shared state (incrementing a counter)
 - Calling rate-limited APIs
 - Excel Online (write conflicts on parallel writes)

When to keep parallel (default):
 - Independent operations (sending emails to different people)
 - Faster execution
 - No shared state

Apply to each — limits and gotchas

⚠ COMMON ISSUES
  1. Max iterations: 100,000 per Apply to each. Exceeds → flow fails.
  2. Pagination needed for large lists — many connectors cap at 100/256 items per call. Enable pagination in action settings.
  3. Setting variables in parallel loops — race conditions corrupt the variable. Set Concurrency = 1.
  4. Append to array variable in parallel — same race issue. Use sequential mode.
  5. Nested Apply to each — works but slow. Max 8 levels deep.
  6. Empty arrays — Apply to each completes silently (0 iterations). Check length() first if "no items" matters.
  7. Type mismatch — feeding a non-array won't work; wrap in array() or use Select.
  8. Premium connector calls inside loops — counted per call; can blow API limits fast.

The Do until action

Do until (Control > Do until):
 Runs inner actions REPEATEDLY until a condition is true
 Useful for polling, waiting, retry-until-success
 
 Layout:
 Do until
 Condition: [comparison] (true means STOP)
 Change limits:
 Count: max iterations (default 60)
 Timeout: max duration (default PT1H = 1 hour)
 
 [inner actions]
 
 Loop exits when:
 - Condition evaluates to true, OR
 - Count exceeded, OR
 - Timeout elapsed

NOTE: Condition checked AFTER each iteration (do-while)
 → Inner actions always run at least once

Do until — polling pattern

Common use: wait for a long-running operation to finish

Example: Wait for AI Builder model to finish processing

Action: Submit document to AI Builder
 Returns: a job ID

Action: Initialize variable jobStatus = "Running"

Action: Do until
 Condition: variables('jobStatus') is equal to "Complete"
 Count: 30
 Timeout: PT15M (15 minutes)
 
 Action: Delay
 1 minute (don't poll too aggressively)
 
 Action: HTTP GET (or connector action)
 Get job status by ID
 
 Action: Set variable jobStatus = response status

After loop:
 Action: Condition — jobStatus is "Complete"
 If yes: process results
 If no: timeout — handle failure

Do until — limits

SettingDefaultMax
Count (iterations)605000
Timeout (duration)PT1H (1 hour)PT30D (depends on plan)

Timeout format: ISO 8601 duration. PT15M = 15 minutes. PT2H = 2 hours. P1D = 1 day. Always set BOTH safety nets.

Pagination — getting more than the connector default

Most connectors return up to 100 (or 256) rows per call by default.

To get more:
 Click "..." on the action (e.g., Get items, List rows)
 Settings → Pagination: ON
 Threshold: 100 to 100,000

What happens:
 Action internally pages through results
 Returns single combined array (up to threshold)

Limits:
 SharePoint Get items: max 5000
 Dataverse List rows: max 100,000
 Excel List rows: max 5000
 Outlook Get emails: max 250

When to use:
 Always enable for production flows that process datasets

Cost:
 Each underlying page call counts against API limits

▣ EXAMPLE: Convert PDFs to text and email summaries
Trigger: Manually trigger a flow
 Input: folder path (text)

Action: List files in folder
 Path: triggerBody()?['folderPath']
 → Pagination enabled, threshold 5000

Action: Apply to each (file)
 Concurrency: 5 (parallel but not too aggressive)
 
 Action: Condition — file ends with .pdf
 If yes:
 Action: Get file content
 File: item()?['Path']
 
 Action: AI Builder — Extract text from PDF
 Content: outputs of Get file content
 
 Action: Send email
 To: triggerBody()?['user']
 Subject: Summary of @{item()?['Name']}
 Body: @{outputs('Extract_text')?['body']?['responsev2']?['predictionOutput']?['text']}
 
 If no:
 (skip non-PDFs silently)

Worked example — wait for approval status

▣ EXAMPLE: Poll Dataverse row until approved
Trigger: Manual flow with input ticketId

Action: Initialize variable approved = false

Action: Do until
 Condition: variables('approved') is equal to true
 Count: 144 (every 5 min × 12 hours = 144 iterations)
 Timeout: PT12H (12 hours)
 
 Action: Delay
 Count: 5
 Unit: Minute
 
 Action: Get a row by ID (Dataverse)
 Table: Tickets
 Row ID: triggerBody()?['ticketId']
 
 Action: Condition — approval_status = 1 (Approved)
 If yes:
 Set variable approved = true
 If no:
 (continue polling)

After Do until:
 Action: Condition — approved is true
 If yes: proceed with downstream work
 If no: Terminate with status "Failed", message "Timed out"

Breaking out of a loop

No native "break" in Apply to each (unlike Do until).

Workarounds:
 
 1. TERMINATE action inside the loop
 Stops entire flow — works but heavy-handed
 
 2. Use a "skip" boolean variable
 Inside loop, wrap inner work in Condition:
 Condition: variables('shouldStop') = false
 If yes: run normal inner actions
 If no: do nothing
 
 Set shouldStop = true when condition met
 Subsequent iterations no-op
 
 3. Use Filter array BEFORE the loop
 Pre-filter the source array to only what you want
 Apply to each only iterates the wanted subset
 
 4. Use Do until instead
 Build the same logic with explicit condition

For most cases, use approach 3 — filter early, don't loop-and-skip.

Filter array action — pre-loop filtering

Filter array (Data Operation > Filter array):
 Reduces an array to elements matching a condition
 Runs BEFORE Apply to each → fewer iterations

Example:
 Get items (SharePoint): returns ALL items (with pagination)
 Filter array:
 From: Get items output
 Condition: item()?['Status'] is equal to 'Open'
 Apply to each: only Open items now

When better than OData filter:
 - Complex multi-step filtering
 - Filtering on calculated/parsed properties
 - Combining multiple sources

When OData filter is better:
 - Filter is simple
 - Source supports filtering (saves bandwidth)
 - SharePoint Get items: $filter=Status eq 'Open'

Loop performance tips

★ MAKE LOOPS FAST
  1. Filter early — reduce array before looping
  2. Maximize concurrency for independent iterations (default 20)
  3. Use Select for transformations — bulk transform array without loop
  4. Batch external API calls when possible — one call with 100 items vs 100 loops
  5. Cache lookups outside the loop — fetch a reference table once, lookup inside
  6. Avoid nested loops when possible — quadratic performance
  7. Don't update one item per iteration — use Dataverse Bulk operations or HTTP batch
  8. Compose actions are cheap — variables are expensive across iterations

Select action — transform an array

Select (Data Operation > Select):
 Transform each element of array → new shape
 ZERO iterations visible — runs in single action

Example: project rows down to {name, email}

 From: Get rows output
 Map:
 name: item()?['FirstName']
 email: item()?['Email']

Output: array of {name, email} objects

When to use Select over Apply to each:
 Pure transformation (no side effects)
 Building a smaller dataset
 Preparing JSON for an HTTP body
 Generating HTML rows for an email

When to use Apply to each:
 Side effects per item (send email, create row, file upload)
 Conditional logic per item
 Different actions for different items

Loop choice decision tree

NeedUse
Process each item in a known arrayApply to each
Poll until a condition is metDo until
Retry a failing callBuilt-in retry policy + Do until fallback
Transform array without side effectsSelect (no loop)
Reduce array to subsetFilter array (no loop)
Count items in arraylength() expression (no loop)
Sum / aggregate valuesSelect to extract + sum() / max() / min() expressions
★ ON THE EXAM

"Loop over array?" → Apply to each.

"Loop until condition?" → Do until.

"Parallel default for Apply to each?" → 20.

"Max parallel?" → 50.

"Want sequential?" → Concurrency control = 1.

"Modifying shared variable in loop?" → MUST set Concurrency = 1.

"Get more than 100 items?" → Enable pagination.

"Default Do until count?" → 60.

"Default Do until timeout?" → PT1H (1 hour).

"Need to break early?" → Variable flag or Terminate.

"Transform array without side effects?" → Select (no loop needed).

"Reduce array?" → Filter array.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Apply to each iterates a known array; auto-inserted when you pick dynamic content from an array source
  • Use item() to reference the current element inside Apply to each
  • Default concurrency is 20 parallel iterations (max 50)
  • Set concurrency = 1 when modifying shared state (variables, sequential writes)
  • Apply to each max iterations: 100,000 per loop
  • Enable pagination on list actions to fetch beyond default 100/256 limit
  • Do until is a do-while loop: condition checked after iteration
  • Always set both Count and Timeout on Do until as safety nets
  • Use Do until for polling long-running operations (AI Builder, approvals, external APIs)
  • No native "break" — use Filter array first, or variable flag, or Terminate
  • Select transforms arrays without a loop; faster for pure transformations
  • Filter array reduces an array before looping
  • Nested loops work but slow; max 8 levels deep
  • Always filter/aggregate at the source (OData) when possible — most efficient
  • length(), sum(), max(), min() expressions work without loops on arrays

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The heart of RPA is UI automation — telling the robot exactly which button to click, which field to type into. Getting selectors right is the #1 skill that separates flows that work for 5 minutes from flows that run reliably for years. This section covers the core UI automation actions and selector engineering.

The UI automation action group

In PAD: Actions panel → UI automation

Subcategories:
 Data extraction: Get details of UI element, Get details of window
 Form filling: Click UI element, Populate text field, Press button
 Selection: Select menu option, Set checkbox, Set radio button
 Window: Get window, Focus window, Resize, Move, Close
 Wait: Wait for UI element, Wait for window
 Drag & drop: Drag and drop UI element
 Image: Click on image, Wait for image (slower but resilient)

Core pattern:
 1. Wait for UI element (handle slow apps)
 2. Click / Fill / Select that element
 3. Verify result (read back, check next screen)
 
Repeat for each step in the workflow.

Capturing a UI element

When configuring an UI automation action:
 Field: "UI element"
 Click the dropdown
 Option 1: Add UI element
 - Press Ctrl+click to capture
 - Move mouse over target — highlight box appears
 - Click target → captured into UI elements panel
 Option 2: Use an existing UI element (already captured)

Captured info:
 Selector path (window > pane > control)
 Properties: name, control type, ID, class
 Screenshot snapshot for verification

UI elements panel (right side):
 Tree of all captured elements organized by app/window
 Click an element to see/edit its selector
 Rename for clarity ("LoginButton" not "Button1")
 Delete unused elements

Selector structure

A selector is a chain of UI element matchers:

 > window 'Notepad' > document 'Untitled - Notepad'
 
 Means: find a window with title 'Notepad', then a document inside it.

Each level can match by:
 Name "Submit"
 Control type Button, Edit, ComboBox
 Class WindowsForms10.BUTTON.app.0.378734a
 Automation ID btnSubmit
 Process name notepad.exe
 Index [1] (first match)

Attribute syntax in selector editor:
 > button [Name = "Submit"]
 > button [Name ~ ".*Submit.*"] (regex)
 > input [Id = "email"]

Multiple selectors for fallback:
 PAD can have multiple "selectors" per element
 Tries first; falls back to second if no match
 Useful for "Submit" button that might be "OK" in another version

Reliable selectors — engineering tips

★ MAKING SELECTORS ROBUST
  1. Prefer Name or Automation ID over position/index — semantic identifiers don't change
  2. Avoid screen coordinates — windows move and resize
  3. Don't depend on window title containing dates — "Report - July 2025" breaks in August
  4. Use regex for variable titles — ~ "Report - .*" matches any month
  5. Skip intermediate panels when targeting deeply nested elements — but only when the target is uniquely identifiable
  6. Test in different states: maximized, minimized, with/without scroll, different language
  7. Add Wait for UI element before every interaction — never assume the element is ready
  8. Use try/catch (On error) blocks for critical clicks — retry with sleep between

Common UI automation actions

ActionPurpose
Click UI element in windowSingle/double/right click on a control
Populate text field in windowType text into an Edit control
Press button in windowClick a Button control (faster than Click UI element)
Select menu optionPick from a dropdown / menu
Set checkbox / radio buttonToggle a boolean control
Get details of UI elementRead a control's text, state, or property
Wait for UI elementPause flow until element appears/disappears
Focus windowBring a window to foreground
Get window stateCheck if minimized/maximized/normal
Drag and drop UI elementMove object via mouse drag

Wait actions — critical for reliability

UI doesn't react instantly:
 Apps load, animations play, network calls finish
 Without waits, RPA tries to click before button exists → crash

Wait for UI element:
 Appears: pause until element visible
 Disappears: pause until element gone (e.g., loading spinner)
 Timeout: max wait time (seconds)
 
 Example: Wait for "OK" button to appear, max 30 seconds

Wait for window:
 Same idea, but for whole window
 Use when launching apps

Wait (simple delay):
 Pause N seconds — last resort
 Use when no specific element to wait for
 Common: 1-2 second wait after typing, before clicking

DON'T use sleep everywhere:
 Brittle — works on fast machine, fails on slow
 Wait for UI element is more reliable
 
Anti-pattern (avoid):
 Click button
 Wait 5 seconds (hoping next screen loads)
 Click next button (might fail if slow)

Better:
 Click button
 Wait for "Next Page Title" to appear (timeout 30s)
 Click next button

Image-based automation (fallback)

When UI accessibility fails (Java apps, Citrix, remote desktop, games):
 Fall back to image recognition
 
Actions:
 - Click on image
 - Wait for image
 - Get position of image
 - Get pixel color
 - Extract text with OCR

How it works:
 Capture screenshot of target ("Submit" button)
 PAD scans the screen for that image
 Clicks when found

Trade-offs:
 PRO: works on anything visible
 CON: very slow (pixel-by-pixel scan)
 CON: fragile to resolution, theme, font changes
 CON: false matches on similar-looking elements

When to use:
 Last resort — accessibility-blind apps
 Mainframe terminal screens
 Games / kiosk-style UIs
 Remote desktop (HDX/RDP can break selectors)

OCR for reading screens

When you can't access text programmatically (PDF image, scanned doc, screenshot):

Action: Extract text with OCR
 Source: image file, screen region, window
 Engine: Windows OCR (built-in) or Tesseract (open source)
 Output: extracted text variable

Use cases:
 - Read amounts from screen-captured invoices
 - Validate form data displayed in legacy app
 - Extract text from images in PDF

Limits:
 - Accuracy varies with font, size, contrast
 - Numbers often misread (0 vs O, 1 vs l)
 - Tables hard to preserve structure
 - Foreign language requires correct language pack

Better alternatives when available:
 - AI Builder Document Processing (smarter than raw OCR)
 - Adobe PDF tools (cleaner text extraction)

Worked example — automate a legacy invoice entry app

▣ EXAMPLE: Daily invoice entry
Scenario: Vendor sends Excel with 50 invoices daily. Need to enter each into 
legacy desktop "InvoicePro" app.

Flow steps:

1. Action: Read from Excel worksheet
 File: vendor.xlsx
 Worksheet: Invoices
 → CreatesVariable: ExcelData (datatable)

2. Action: Launch application
 App: C:\\Program Files\\InvoicePro\\InvoicePro.exe
 → CreatesVariable: InvoiceProWindow

3. Action: Wait for window
 Title: "InvoicePro - Login"
 Timeout: 30 seconds

4. Action: Populate text field
 UI element: Login window > Username field
 Text: %EnvUsername%

5. Action: Populate text field
 UI element: Login window > Password field
 Text: %EnvPassword%

6. Action: Press button
 UI element: Login window > Login button

7. Action: Wait for UI element
 UI element: Main window > "Welcome" label
 Timeout: 30 seconds

8. Action: For each row in ExcelData

 8a. Action: Click UI element
 UI element: Main window > "New Invoice" button

 8b. Action: Populate text field
 UI element: New Invoice form > Vendor field
 Text: %CurrentItem['Vendor']%

 8c. Action: Populate text field
 UI element: New Invoice form > Amount field
 Text: %CurrentItem['Amount']%

 8d. Action: Populate text field
 UI element: New Invoice form > Date field
 Text: %CurrentItem['Date']%

 8e. Action: Press button
 UI element: New Invoice form > Save button

 8f. Action: Wait for UI element
 UI element: Main window > "Invoice saved" toast
 Disappears: True
 Timeout: 10 seconds

9. Action: Close application
 App window: InvoiceProWindow

Error handling in UI automation

UI automation FAILS regularly:
 - Network slow → element doesn't appear in time
 - Pop-up dialog steals focus → wrong window targeted
 - App crashed → window doesn't exist
 - User changed UI scaling → selector misses

Use On error blocks:

Action: On error
 → wraps subsequent actions in try/catch

Within block, if any action fails:
 On error subflow runs (recovery logic)
 Or: continue to next action (silent failure)
 Or: stop the flow with custom error message

Common recovery:
 - Take screenshot for debugging
 - Close all app windows (cleanup)
 - Send email alert with error details
 - Restart the app
 - Retry the failed step (max 3 times)

Built-in retry:
 Some actions have a "Retry policy" in Advanced
 Number of retries + delay between
 Cleaner than manual try/catch for transient failures

Send keys (keyboard shortcuts)

Action: Send keys
 Sends keyboard input to active window
 Useful for shortcuts not exposed in UI elements
 
 Syntax:
 {Tab} — Tab key
 {Enter} — Enter
 {Esc} — Escape
 {F5} — F5 function key
 ^c — Ctrl+C
 %{F4} — Alt+F4
 +A — Shift+A
 
 Plain text: "Hello" → types those characters

Use cases:
 - Keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+S, Ctrl+P)
 - Tab through forms when UI elements aren't easily captured
 - Press Enter to submit a search
 - Alt+F4 to close a dialog with no Close button

Caution:
 - Send keys hits ACTIVE window — make sure target is focused first
 - Use Focus window action immediately before
 - Modifier syntax differs from regular typing
★ ON THE EXAM

"Identify a UI control?" → Selector (window > pane > control).

"Wait until element appears?" → Wait for UI element.

"App without accessibility?" → Image-based actions.

"Read screen text?" → OCR.

"Keyboard shortcut?" → Send keys.

"Recover from failure?" → On error block.

"Multiple ways to identify same element?" → Multiple selectors with fallback.

"Element location changes?" → Avoid index/coords; use Name or Automation ID.

"Variable window title (date in title)?" → Regex selector matching pattern.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • UI automation actions click, type, and read controls in any Windows app
  • Capture UI elements via Ctrl+click during configuration
  • Selectors are paths: window > pane > control, matched by Name/ID/Class
  • Prefer Name or Automation ID over index for stable selectors
  • Use regex selectors for variable titles ("Report - .*")
  • Multiple selectors per element provide fallback paths
  • Always Wait for UI element before interacting — never assume readiness
  • Wait for element to appear OR disappear (good for spinners)
  • Image-based actions are fallback for inaccessible apps (Citrix, Java, games)
  • OCR reads text from screenshots when no programmatic access
  • Use On error blocks for robust retry and recovery
  • Send keys for keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+C, Tab, F5)
  • Always Focus window before Send keys to target correct app
  • Selectors break with UI changes — version your flows alongside the app
  • Document selectors with clear names and screenshots

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Web automation in Power Automate Desktop handles tasks against websites — scraping data, filling forms, navigating pages. It's essential when a service has no API but exposes a web UI. The PL-500 exam tests browser automation patterns.

Browser support

Power Automate Desktop supports automation in:
 - Microsoft Edge (built-in)
 - Google Chrome (extension required)
 - Mozilla Firefox (extension required)
 - Internet Explorer (legacy; deprecated)

Browser extensions:
 Install during PAD setup, or manually:
 - Edge: Microsoft Edge Add-ons store
 - Chrome: Chrome Web Store
 - Firefox: Mozilla Add-ons

After install:
 Extension communicates with PAD
 Captures elements during web recording
 Performs actions during playback

Check extension status:
 PAD console → Settings → Browser extensions
 Shows which browsers are configured

Launching a browser

Three approaches:

1. Launch new browser instance:
 Action: Launch new Edge / Chrome / Firefox / IE
 PAD opens a fresh browser
 Returns browser reference variable
 Closes when flow ends (or close action)

2. Attach to existing browser:
 Action: Attach to existing browser tab
 Choose by title or URL pattern
 Useful: continue automation on already-open page

3. Run automation in InPrivate / Incognito:
 Same launch action; with privacy option
 Cleaner: no history; no auto-login from cookies
 Useful for testing automation

Launch options:
 URL to navigate to
 Window state: Normal / Maximized / Minimized
 Wait for page load: yes (default)

Browser reference variable:
 Pass to all subsequent browser actions
 Examples: %Browser%
 
 Each browser instance has unique reference
 Multiple browsers possible in same flow

Navigating pages

Navigate to URL:
 Action: Navigate to web page
 Browser: %Browser%
 URL: https://example.com/page

Page navigation actions:
 Go back (navigate back in history)
 Go forward (navigate forward)
 Refresh page
 Close web browser

Wait for page load:
 Action: Wait for web page to load
 Useful when page slow

Get current URL / title:
 Action: Get details of web browser
 Output: URL, title, current page metadata

Handle pop-ups and dialogs:
 Most JavaScript alerts auto-handled
 Browser dialogs (download, save) may need explicit handling
 Use UI automation actions for dialog windows

Interacting with elements

Click element:
 Action: Click element on web page
 Browser: %Browser%
 Web element: select from panel
 Click type: Left / Right / Double / Mouse hover

Fill text field:
 Action: Fill text field on web page
 Browser: %Browser%
 Web element: text input field
 Text: %TextToFill%
 Emulate typing: yes (slower; more human-like) / no

Get value from element:
 Action: Get text on web page
 Browser: %Browser%
 Web element: target
 Output: variable

Set checkbox state:
 Action: Set check box state on web page
 Browser: %Browser%
 Web element: checkbox
 State: Checked / Unchecked

Select option in dropdown:
 Action: Set drop-down list value on web page
 Browser: %Browser%
 Web element: select element
 Option to select: text or index

Click links:
 Action: Click link on web page
 Same as Click element; tailored for anchor tags

Submit forms:
 Action: Submit form on web page
 Browser: %Browser%
 Form: web element

Hover over element:
 Action: Hover mouse over element on web page
 Browser: %Browser%
 Web element: target
 Useful: trigger dropdown menus on hover

Web selectors

Browser actions use web-specific selectors

Selector types:
 CSS selector: button#submit
 XPath: //button[@id='submit']
 Both supported

Where to get selectors:
 Web recorder captures automatically
 Or manually inspect element in browser (F12 dev tools)
 Then enter selector in PAD's web element setup

CSS selector examples:
 button#submitBtn // ID
 .submit-class // class
 form button // descendant button in form
 input[type='email'] // attribute
 div.product:nth-child(2) // nth child

XPath examples:
 //button[@id='submitBtn']
 //form//button
 //input[@type='email']
 //a[contains(text(), 'Login')]

Stable web selectors:
 Use IDs when available
 Avoid: deeply nested paths
 Avoid: positional ([2]) without context
 Use: data attributes (data-test="login-btn") if available
 Add fallback selectors

Web element panel:
 Right panel → Web elements tab
 Browse, edit, test selectors
 Highlight in browser to verify

Web scraping

Scraping = extract data from web pages
Common automation use case

Scrape single value:
 Get text on web page
 Or: Get attribute of element

Scrape multiple items (lists):
 Action: Extract data from web page
 Type: Table / List / Form
 Selects multiple matching elements
 Returns: Datatable variable

Extract data wizard:
 Click "Extract data" while web recorder active
 Click first matching element on page
 PAD prompts: "Is this similar element?" click next
 After 2 clicks: PAD identifies pattern
 Repeat to expand: more rows, multiple columns
 Save → datatable variable

Pagination:
 Often results span multiple pages
 Pattern:
 Loop until: no more pages
 Extract data from current page
 Append to overall results
 Click "Next" button
 Wait for page load

Iterate scraped data:
 Output is Datatable
 Use For each loop:
 Action: For each row in Datatable
 Variable: %CurrentRow%
 Access columns: %CurrentRow["columnName"]%

Best practices:
 Respect robots.txt
 Rate limit: don't hammer the server
 Test with small samples first
 Handle empty pages gracefully
 Consider Terms of Service before automating

Running JavaScript

When UI element clicks aren't enough:

Action: Run JavaScript function on web page
Browser: %Browser%
JavaScript function: 
 function() {
 // your JS code here
 return result;
 }

Examples:

Set value in tricky input:
 function() {
 document.getElementById('inputField').value = 'new value';
 document.getElementById('inputField').dispatchEvent(new Event('change'));
 }

Click via JS (when UI element fails):
 function() {
 document.querySelector('button.tricky').click();
 }

Get all links on page:
 function() {
 return Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('a')).map(a => a.href);
 }

Wait for AJAX:
 Function that polls DOM until expected element appears
 Return when ready

Scroll to element:
 function() {
 document.getElementById('target').scrollIntoView();
 }

Output is captured in return value
PAD wraps with auto Promise handling if async

Working with web frames

Iframes (frames) embed pages within pages
Each frame has its own DOM and document context

Common in:
 - Banking sites (security)
 - Embedded widgets (Google Maps, YouTube)
 - Complex web apps

Web automation must:
 1. Detect iframe presence
 2. Switch context to iframe
 3. Find elements inside iframe
 4. Switch back to parent if needed

Web recorder usually handles automatically
Manual editing of selectors may need frame reference

Cross-frame issues:
 Element search across frames may fail
 Verify which frame contains your target

Test approach:
 Open browser dev tools
 Inspect target element
 Check if inside iframe (search for frame ancestors)
 Adjust selector accordingly

Common web automation mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Browser extension not installed — actions silently fail
  2. Wrong browser launched — actions look for Chrome but Edge opened
  3. Page load not waited — element not yet rendered
  4. Iframe ignored — selector finds nothing
  5. Brittle XPath — breaks on minor HTML change
  6. Anti-bot protections (Cloudflare, reCAPTCHA) — block automation
  7. Rate limiting — server rejects rapid requests
  8. Pop-up windows / new tabs not handled
  9. Login session expired — automation fails mid-flow
  10. JavaScript-heavy SPA — DOM changes dynamically; need explicit waits
★ ON THE EXAM

"Browser support?" → Edge, Chrome, Firefox, IE.

"Extension required?" → Yes for Chrome/Firefox; built-in to Edge.

"Launch action?" → "Launch new Edge / Chrome / Firefox / IE".

"Navigate to URL?" → Navigate to web page action.

"Fill form?" → Fill text field on web page.

"Click button on page?" → Click element on web page.

"Read text?" → Get text on web page.

"Scrape table?" → Extract data from web page action.

"Pagination?" → Loop with Click Next button + Wait for page load.

"Run JavaScript?" → Run JavaScript function on web page.

"Selector types?" → CSS or XPath.

"Web vs desktop elements?" → Different; web uses CSS/XPath.

"Iframes?" → Frames embed pages; selectors must target frame context.

"Web recorder?" → Captures elements while you browse pages.

"Anti-bot blocks?" → CAPTCHA, IP rate limits; may need different approach.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • PAD supports Edge (built-in), Chrome, Firefox, IE (legacy)
  • Chrome and Firefox need browser extension installed
  • Launch browser action creates session; reference variable for all subsequent actions
  • Web selectors use CSS or XPath syntax
  • Common actions: navigate, click, fill, get text, set checkbox, select dropdown
  • Extract data from web page: scrapes tables / lists into Datatable
  • Web recorder: capture elements while browsing
  • Stable selectors: prefer IDs, data attributes, named classes; avoid positional indexes
  • Iframes: each frame has separate DOM; selectors must target correctly
  • JavaScript action: run custom JS in browser for complex DOM manipulation
  • Pagination pattern: loop with "click Next" + wait for page load
  • Anti-bot protections (CAPTCHA, reCAPTCHA) block standard automation
  • Always wait for page load before interacting with elements
  • Handle pop-ups, new tabs, dialogs explicitly
  • Best practices: rate limit requests, respect robots.txt, test small samples
  • SPA (single-page apps) need explicit waits for dynamic DOM changes

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Real enterprise automation usually mixes cloud and desktop flows. Cloud handles orchestration, APIs, and approvals; desktop handles legacy app interactions and UI automation. The hybrid pattern is on the PL-500 exam and is the heart of modern RPA.

The hybrid pattern

Cloud + Desktop = Hybrid automation

Why combine:
 Cloud excels at:
 - Triggering on events (email, schedule, item create)
 - Calling cloud APIs
 - Approvals, notifications
 - Multi-step orchestration
 - 24/7 reliability
 
 Desktop excels at:
 - Legacy app UI
 - Excel macros and local files
 - Apps without APIs
 - Local-only systems
 - Custom Windows software

Hybrid combines:
 Cloud orchestrates the workflow
 Calls desktop flow for legacy parts
 Cloud notifies / logs after desktop completes
 Hidden complexity: legacy systems automated transparently

Architecture:
 Trigger → Cloud actions → Run Desktop Flow → Cloud actions → Done

How cloud calls desktop

Cloud flow uses connector: Power Automate Desktop (Microsoft)

Action: "Run a flow built with Power Automate Desktop"

Configuration:
 Run Mode:
 Attended (user logged in)
 Unattended (no user; premium required)
 
 Machine:
 Specific machine name
 Or: Machine group (load balanced)
 
 Desktop Flow:
 Select from list of published flows
 (Must be saved/uploaded to cloud)
 
 Inputs:
 Match the desktop flow's input variables
 Pass dynamic content from cloud flow
 
 Connection:
 Authenticated connection to PAD
 Service account or user account

Action waits for desktop flow to complete
Returns desktop flow's output variables
Available as dynamic content downstream

Desktop flow inputs and outputs

Make desktop flow callable with parameters

In PAD:
 File menu → Input/Output variables
 Or right panel → Inputs/Outputs

Define Inputs:
 Each input has:
 Variable name
 Data type (Text/Number/Boolean/Date/File)
 External name (shown to cloud caller)
 Description
 Default value (optional)
 Required: yes/no

Define Outputs:
 Variable name (created during flow)
 External name (returned to cloud caller)
 Description

Pattern:
 Inputs: data the desktop flow needs (e.g., customer name)
 Process: desktop flow performs work
 Outputs: results (e.g., confirmation number, error message)

In cloud flow:
 Pass input values
 After "Run desktop flow" action: outputs available as dynamic content
 Use outputs in subsequent cloud actions

Machine setup

Register a Windows machine with Power Automate

Steps:
 1. Install Power Automate Desktop
 2. Sign in to PAD
 3. PAD console → Machines → Register
 4. Provide machine name
 5. Machine appears in Power Automate Admin Center

Machine modes:
 Attended:
 User logged in
 PAD runs visible
 Used for: testing, hand-off scenarios
 Free
 
 Unattended:
 Machine runs without user logged in
 Power Automate signs in service account
 Runs PAD in background session
 Premium license required

Configuring unattended:
 Power Automate Admin Center → Machines
 Pick machine → Edit settings
 Toggle "Unattended" on
 Configure service account credentials
 Schedule machine restart cycles for stability

Machine groups:
 Pool of unattended machines
 Cloud flow selects machine group
 Load balances across available machines
 Useful: high-volume desktop flows
 Failover if one machine down

Authentication and connections

Connecting cloud flow to desktop flow:

Connection types:
 Personal (your account):
 Uses your credentials
 Works for testing
 Breaks if you leave company
 
 Service account:
 Dedicated account for automation
 Doesn't break with personnel changes
 Recommended for production
 
 Machine credentials:
 For unattended mode
 Stored in Azure Key Vault or PAD settings
 Used when machine starts unattended session

Setting up service account:
 Create dedicated Azure AD user
 License with Power Automate Premium
 Sign in to PAD on target machine
 Configure for unattended:
 Settings → Machine settings
 Allow user to sign in unattended

Credentials in flows:
 Don't hardcode passwords in actions
 Use Power Automate's credential management
 Or: Azure Key Vault for sensitive secrets

Permissions:
 Service account needs access to:
 PAD (Power Platform license)
 Target apps on the machine
 Network resources / file shares
 Required Windows permissions

Common hybrid patterns

Pattern 1: Cloud-orchestrated legacy data entry

Trigger: SharePoint item created (cloud)
Cloud Actions:
 Get item details
 Look up customer in cloud CRM
 Determine if legacy entry needed
 If yes:
 Run desktop flow: EnterInLegacySystem
 Pass: customer ID, item details
 Wait for completion
 Get desktop flow outputs (confirmation number)
 Update SharePoint item with confirmation
 Email customer

Desktop flow (called):
 Open legacy app
 Click New Entry
 Fill fields with passed inputs
 Save
 Capture confirmation
 Return confirmation as output

Pattern 2: Scheduled batch with desktop

Trigger: Recurrence nightly at 2am (cloud)
Cloud Actions:
 Get list of pending records from Dataverse
 For each record:
 Run desktop flow: ProcessOneRecord
 Pass record details
 Wait for completion
 Compose summary
 Email admin: "Processed N records"

Desktop flow (called per record):
 Open legacy ERP
 Enter record data
 Run macros / calculations
 Save
 Return: processed status

Concurrency:
 Multiple cloud flow runs in parallel possible
 Each calls desktop flow on different machine in group
 Effectively batch processing in parallel

Pattern 3: Approval triggers desktop

Trigger: PowerApps button (cloud)
Cloud Actions:
 Start approval (manager approval)
 Wait for response
 If approved:
 Run desktop flow: ProcessApproved
 Pass: approved item details, approver name
 Wait for completion
 Else:
 Update record as rejected
 Notify requester

Desktop flow (called after approval):
 Apply approval in legacy system
 Generate confirmation document
 Save document to OneDrive
 Return: document path

Cloud after desktop:
 Send confirmation email with document link
 Update Dataverse with confirmation
 Log audit trail

Error handling across cloud and desktop

Both layers need error handling

Cloud side:
 Wrap "Run desktop flow" action in Scope
 Catch via Run After Failed
 Capture: error message, run ID, machine name

Desktop side:
 Use try-catch logic in subflows (if/error structure)
 Take screenshot on failure
 Set output variable: success/failure + error message
 Return cleanly even on failure (don't crash)

Communication:
 Desktop returns output variable indicating success
 Cloud reads outputs:
 if outputs.success = true → continue
 if outputs.success = false → handle error, notify, retry

Retry logic:
 Cloud can retry desktop flow on failure
 Configure: max attempts, backoff between attempts
 Or: alternate machine if first one is unhealthy

Logging:
 Desktop flow logs to file
 Cloud flow logs to audit table
 Combined: full traceable history
 Run history in Power Automate cloud aggregates both

Worked example — invoice processing hybrid

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Invoice OCR + legacy entry
// Goal: Process invoice emails end-to-end
// 1. Cloud detects email
// 2. AI extracts data
// 3. Approval

Common hybrid mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Production flows fail — API errors, throttling, timeouts, bad data. Without error handling, a flow either silently corrupts data or stops running. Power Automate's error handling patterns are tested on the PL-100 and PL-500 exams.

How actions can fail

Action statuses after running:
 Succeeded — completed normally
 Failed — error during execution
 Skipped — Run After conditions not met
 Timed out — exceeded action timeout
 Cancelled — flow was cancelled mid-run

Common failure causes:
 Connector throttling (HTTP 429)
 Service unavailable (HTTP 5xx)
 Authentication expired (HTTP 401)
 Bad data (HTTP 400)
 Missing fields (null reference)
 Permission denied (HTTP 403)
 Network timeout
 Rate limit exceeded
 Invalid expression syntax

By default:
 If any action fails, the flow stops
 Subsequent actions don't run
 Flow marked as Failed
 No notification unless configured

Run After configuration

Run After = controls when an action runs based on previous action's status

Configuration:
 Click ... menu on action → Settings → Configure Run After
 Pick: which previous action to depend on
 Check: which statuses trigger this action
 Succeeded
 Failed
 Skipped
 Timed out (only some actions)
 
 Multi-select allowed

Examples:

Default behavior:
 Run After: Succeeded only
 Standard sequential flow

Error handler:
 Run After: Failed
 Catches errors from previous action

Always run:
 Run After: Succeeded OR Failed OR Skipped
 Cleanup or logging that should always happen

Continue on error:
 Run After: Succeeded OR Failed
 Continues processing even if previous failed
 Useful: optional steps that shouldn't block main path

Within Apply to each:
 Each iteration runs independently
 One failed iteration doesn't stop others (unless using Terminate)

Try-catch with Scope

Power Automate pattern: Scope action + Run After

Structure:
 Scope: "Try"
 Action 1
 Action 2
 Action 3

 Scope: "Catch"
 Configure Run After: "Try" → Failed
 Action: log error, notify, etc.

 Scope: "Finally"
 Configure Run After: "Try" → Succeeded, Failed, Skipped
 Action: cleanup, always runs

Behavior:
 If all actions in Try succeed → Try = Succeeded
 If any action in Try fails → Try = Failed (Catch runs)
 Finally always runs

Information available in Catch:
 outputs('Try') — full scope output
 result('Try') — array of action results
 
 Iterate via Apply to each on result('Try')
 Each element has: name, startTime, endTime, status, error

Better pattern:
 Use Compose to get the failing action and error message
 Send detailed alert with context

Standard advanced setup:
 Multiple Scopes for different failure paths
 Catch for transient errors → retry
 Catch for permanent errors → log + escalate

Built-in retry policy

Power Automate has automatic retry for transient failures

Default policy:
 Each action retries up to 4 times automatically
 Exponential backoff between retries
 Total retry duration: ~30 seconds default
 Applies to specific HTTP errors (429, 5xx)

Configuration per action:
 Click ... menu → Settings → Retry Policy
 
 Options:
 Default — exponential, 4 retries
 None — no retry
 Fixed — fixed interval
 Exponential — exponential backoff

 Fixed:
 Count: 4 (default)
 Interval: PT20S (20 sec)
 
 Exponential:
 Count: 4
 Min interval: PT5S
 Max interval: PT1H

When to disable retry:
 - Idempotent issues (each retry creates new records)
 - Network operations that already retry internally
 - User-triggered actions where speed matters

When to extend retry:
 - Long-running batch jobs
 - APIs with known instability
 - Flows handling temporary outages

Manual retry (alternative):
 Wrap action in Do until
 Retry counter variable
 Custom backoff logic

Custom retry with Do until

For complex retry scenarios beyond built-in:

Pattern:
 Initialize variable: retry_count = 0
 Initialize variable: success = false
 
 Do until: success equals true OR retry_count > 5
 Scope "Attempt":
 [actions to retry]
 Set: success = true
 
 Scope "OnFail":
 Run After Attempt: Failed
 Increment retry_count
 Delay: 2^retry_count seconds (exponential backoff)
 
 After loop:
 If success: continue normally
 Else: log final failure, notify

Use cases:
 - API that needs specific retry conditions
 - Retry only on specific error types
 - Different backoff than default
 - Logging each retry attempt

Best practice: limit max retries to prevent infinite loops
Always include explicit exit conditions

Terminate action

Terminate = stop the flow explicitly with a status

Action: Terminate

Configuration:
 Status:
 Succeeded — flow ends successfully (even if conditional logic detected an issue)
 Failed — flow ends with failed status (counts as failure)
 Cancelled — flow ends in cancelled state

 Code (for Failed/Cancelled):
 Optional error code
 e.g., "InvalidInput", "BusinessRuleViolation"
 
 Message (for Failed/Cancelled):
 Human-readable description
 Shown in run history

Use cases:

Early exit on validation:
 Condition: missing required field
 Yes: Terminate Failed with message "Required field X missing"

Conditional success:
 Condition: input was a no-op (record already processed)
 Yes: Terminate Succeeded with message "No action needed"

Detect business rule violation:
 Condition: amount exceeds maximum
 Yes: Terminate Failed with code "AmountTooHigh"

After Terminate:
 Flow stops immediately
 All subsequent actions are Skipped
 Final status as specified

Pairs with: Send notification of termination
 Wrap Terminate in Scope; send email before terminating

Idempotency

Idempotency = running the same action multiple times has same effect as running it once

Why important:
 Retries can cause duplicates
 Network glitches may run action twice
 Flow might re-fire on identical trigger event

Patterns for idempotent design:

Pattern 1: Check before create
 Before "Create item":
 Get items where ExternalKey = current key
 If found: skip create; use existing
 If not found: create new

Pattern 2: Upsert (update if exists, else create)
 Many connectors support "Upsert" actions
 Dataverse: "Upsert a row"
 Updates if exists; creates if new

Pattern 3: External keys
 Each created item has unique external reference
 Future retries find existing record by key
 No duplicates

Pattern 4: Audit log
 Add row to audit table for every action
 Before action: check audit; was it already done?
 After action: log completion
 Retries find prior log entry, skip

Pattern 5: Idempotency tokens
 Pass unique token (GUID) per attempt
 Service uses token to deduplicate
 Common in payment systems

Design for retries from start
Saves significant headaches in production

Failure notifications

Configure how you find out about failures

Built-in:
 Power Automate sends owner an email if flow fails repeatedly
 Configurable in flow settings

Custom notifications:
 Wrap critical actions in Scope
 Add Catch Scope (Run After Failed)
 Inside: send email, post to Teams, etc.

Notification content:
 Flow name
 Run ID (for log lookup)
 Failed action name
 Error message
 Time of failure
 Trigger data (if helpful)
 Link to run history

Example Catch action:
 Send email to admin@company.com
 Subject: "FLOW FAILED: " + concat(workflow()?['tags/flowDisplayName'], ' at ', utcNow())
 Body: 
 "Flow: " + workflow()?['tags/flowDisplayName']
 "Run: " + workflow()?['run/id']
 "Error: " + body('Failed_action')?['error']
 "Link: " + concat('https://make.powerautomate.com/...', workflow()?['run/id'])

Workflow expressions:
 workflow() returns current flow context
 Available properties:
 tags/flowDisplayName
 run/id
 name (flow name)
 type
 triggerName

Best practices:
 Don't spam admins on every flaky run
 Group notifications by severity
 Include enough context to debug
 Auto-retry first; notify after permanent failures

Common error handling mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. No error handling at all — silent failures in production
  2. Catching errors but not logging — debugging impossible
  3. Notification on every failure — alert fatigue
  4. No idempotency — retries create duplicates
  5. Long-running flow without intermediate checkpoints
  6. Retry loop without max — infinite retries on persistent failure
  7. Ignoring built-in retry policy — manual retries when built-in works
  8. Terminate Failed at end of catch — flow still proceeds; use Run After
  9. Hardcoded admin emails in alerts — break when person leaves
  10. No timeout on Do until retry loop — runs forever
★ ON THE EXAM

"Run After options?" → Succeeded, Failed, Skipped, Timed out.

"Where to configure?" → Action ... menu → Settings → Configure Run After.

"Try-catch?" → Scope (try) + Scope (catch with Run After Failed).

"Finally?" → Scope with Run After Succeeded OR Failed OR Skipped.

"Built-in retry?" → Default 4 retries with exponential backoff.

"Retry policies?" → Default, None, Fixed, Exponential.

"Configure retry?" → Action ... menu → Settings → Retry Policy.

"Custom retry?" → Do until with retry counter + delay.

"Stop flow?" → Terminate action (Succeeded/Failed/Cancelled).

"Validate inputs?" → Compose + Condition + Terminate Failed.

"Idempotency?" → Check before create; use external keys; upsert pattern.

"Get failed action details?" → outputs('ScopeName') with filter on status.

"Flow run ID?" → workflow()?['run/id'].

"Flow name?" → workflow()?['tags/flowDisplayName'].

"Failure notification?" → Catch Scope with Send email action.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Actions have 4 statuses: Succeeded, Failed, Skipped, Timed out
  • Run After controls when an action runs based on previous action's status
  • Configure via action ... menu → Settings → Configure Run After
  • Try-catch pattern: Scope (try) + Scope (catch with Run After Failed)
  • Add Finally Scope with Run After all statuses for cleanup
  • Built-in retry: default 4 retries with exponential backoff for transient errors
  • Configure retry per action: Default, None, Fixed, Exponential
  • Terminate action: stop flow with status (Succeeded/Failed/Cancelled) + message
  • Idempotency: design flows to be safe to retry (check before create, upsert, external keys)
  • Custom retry: Do until with counter + delay for complex backoff logic
  • Failure notifications: wrap critical actions; on failure, alert admin/team
  • Get failure details: outputs('Scope') with filter for failed actions
  • Workflow expressions: workflow()?['run/id'], workflow()?['tags/flowDisplayName']
  • Always log errors to a persistent location (audit table, email, Teams)
  • Best practices: idempotent design, explicit retry limits, contextual error messages, no alert spam

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Once flows run in production, you need to know they're working — and quickly find out when they're not. Power Automate provides run history, analytics, Process Advisor, and admin dashboards. The PL-100 and PL-500 exams test monitoring tools.

Run history

Run history = log of every flow execution

Access:
 make.powerautomate.com → My flows → click flow → 28-day history (default)
 Filter by: All / Running / Succeeded / Failed / Cancelled

Each run shows:
 Start time
 Duration
 Status
 Trigger event (what caused it)

Click into a run:
 See every action step-by-step
 Each step has:
 Status (color-coded)
 Inputs (what was passed)
 Outputs (what was produced)
 Duration
 Error message (if failed)

Step debugging:
 Expand step → see actual values used
 Verify expressions evaluated correctly
 Find where flow diverged from expectation
 Most powerful debugging tool

Time limits:
 28-day run history retention (free tier)
 Premium: 90 days
 Archived: export to longer-term storage if needed

Resubmit and cancel

Resubmit a failed run:
 Run history → click failed run → "Resubmit" button
 Flow runs again with same trigger data
 Useful after fixing connector issues or transient problems

Cancel a running flow:
 Run history → click running flow → Cancel button
 Stops execution mid-flow
 Use when: flow stuck, wrong data, manual intervention needed

Manual rerun:
 For instant flows: just trigger again
 For scheduled: wait for next schedule or trigger manually

Bulk resubmit:
 Select multiple failed runs
 Resubmit all selected
 Useful: after fixing systemic issue affecting many flows

Flow analytics

Built-in analytics for each flow

Access:
 Flow detail page → Analytics tab
 Or: Power Automate Admin Center → Analytics

Metrics tracked:
 - Run count (total / per day)
 - Success rate
 - Failure breakdown by error type
 - Average duration
 - Throttling incidents
 - Connector usage

Charts:
 - Runs over time
 - Success vs failure trend
 - Top errors
 - Performance trends

Use cases:
 - Verify SLA compliance
 - Detect performance regression
 - Find flow that suddenly started failing
 - Plan capacity for high-volume scenarios

Limitations:
 - Aggregated; specific run details need run history
 - 28-day window typical
 - Some metrics require Power Automate Premium

Power Automate Admin Center

Admin Center = centralized management for IT admins

Access:
 admin.powerplatform.microsoft.com → Environments → select env → Power Automate

Capabilities:
 Environment-wide flow inventory
 See all flows in tenant/environment
 Track ownership; succession planning
 Disable / enable flows
 Manage connections and references
 
 Analytics:
 Tenant-wide success rates
 Top connectors by usage
 Top users by flow count
 Throttling and quota usage
 
 Quota management:
 Per-environment limits
 Per-user limits
 Premium tier consumption
 
 DLP (Data Loss Prevention):
 Policies for connector usage
 Business vs non-business data categories
 Block sensitive connector combinations

Audit logging:
 Track flow creation, modification, deletion
 User access events
 Connection changes
 
 Available in Microsoft 365 audit log
 Compliance Center → Audit

Process Advisor / Process Mining

Process Advisor = visualize and analyze actual user processes
 Separate feature within Power Automate
 Some features require Power Automate Premium

Two modes:

Task Mining:
 Records user activities on their PC
 Builds map of common task patterns
 Identifies repetitive sequences
 Suggests automation opportunities

Process Mining:
 Analyzes system event logs
 Discovers actual process flows (vs documented)
 Identifies bottlenecks and variations
 Compares ideal vs actual

Use cases:
 - Find automation candidates ("we do this same thing 1000 times")
 - Optimize existing processes
 - Compliance: detect deviation from defined process
 - Bottleneck analysis: where do tasks get stuck?

Output:
 - Process maps with statistics
 - Heatmaps showing common paths
 - Time analysis (how long each step takes)
 - Variation analysis (different ways tasks performed)

When to use:
 - Before automation: identify what's worth automating
 - After automation: verify improvement
 - Compliance audits: process conformance
 - Continuous improvement programs

Notifications and alerts

Built-in notifications:

Flow owner alerts:
 Default: email if flow fails repeatedly
 Configurable in flow settings
 Can disable per-flow

Failure threshold:
 After X failures in Y time period
 Notifies owner via email
 Default: 4 failures in 24 hours

Custom alerts (build your own):
 Wrap critical actions in Scope
 Catch with Run After Failed
 Send to: email, Teams, SMS (premium), webhook

Power Automate mobile app:
 Notifications for: flow failures, approval requests
 Configurable: turn off for non-urgent flows

Connection alerts:
 If connection breaks (expired, revoked):
 Flow fails on first use after break
 Owner emailed about broken connection
 Visible in Connections page (red status)

Best practices:
 - Critical flows: aggressive monitoring (immediate alerts)
 - Routine flows: digest alerts (daily summary)
 - Personal automation: minimal alerts (just to owner)

Debugging step-by-step

Common debugging workflow:

1. Trigger fires; flow starts running
2. Open run history
3. Click latest run; expand actions
4. For each step:
 - Check status (green/red)
 - View inputs (what came in)
 - View outputs (what came out)
 - Compare with expected

Common debug tactics:

Add Compose actions:
 Insert "Compose" with expression to inspect
 Output visible in run history
 Like "console.log" for flows

Test step-by-step:
 Run flow → check each step's output
 Iterate: fix expression → re-test
 Faster than running entire flow

Use sample data:
 Trigger has "Test" button with sample data
 Manually set up test scenarios
 Don't need real events to test

Repeat failed scenarios:
 Resubmit failed runs after fixing issue
 Or: copy trigger data; trigger flow manually

Check logs:
 Run history is primary log
 Audit log for security events
 Connector logs for service-side issues

Use Debug mode (PAD):
 In Power Automate Desktop: step-through mode
 Run one action at a time
 Inspect variables as flow progresses

When stuck:
 Compose action with full step output
 Print intermediate values to test expressions
 Reduce complexity; isolate failing part

 Variables at each step (limited; not full)

 Status: Failed

 On the machine: PAD console → Flow Runs
 See full local execution log
 Screenshots captured at error points

Logging from desktop flow:
 Build in: Set variable to log message + Append to file
 Or: Use SharePoint connector to log to centralized list
 Or: Take screenshots periodically

Machine health monitoring:
 Admin Center → Machines
 Status: Online / Offline / Disconnected
 Last seen timestamp
 Active runs count
 Alert when machine offline > X minutes
