Common monitoring mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. No alerting on failure — production issues unnoticed
  2. Alert fatigue — too many alerts = ignored
  3. No audit trail — can't reconstruct what happened
  4. Relying only on 28-day history — compliance needs longer
  5. Not tracking machine health — desktop flows silently fail
  6. Connection expirations — flow stops; owner notified late
  7. No SLA tracking — don't know if automation hitting targets
  8. Logs scattered — combining cloud + desktop + audit hard
  9. Resubmitting non-idempotent flows — creates duplicates
  10. Ignoring throttling warnings — flows slow / fail silently
★ ON THE EXAM

"View flow runs?" → Run history tab on flow detail page.

"Default retention?" → 28 days free; 90 days premium.

"Step-by-step inputs/outputs?" → Click into run; expand each action.

"Rerun failed?" → Resubmit button in run history.

"Stop running flow?" → Cancel button in run history.

"Flow-level metrics?" → Analytics tab on flow detail page.

"Tenant-wide management?" → Power Automate Admin Center (admin.powerplatform.microsoft.com).

"Find automation opportunities?" → Process Advisor (Task Mining or Process Mining).

"Audit creation/modification?" → Microsoft 365 audit log via Compliance Center.

"DLP policies?" → Admin Center; restrict connector combinations.

"Default failure alert?" → 4 failures in 24 hours → owner emailed.

"Desktop flow runs?" → My flows → Desktop flows tab → run history.

"Machine status?" → Admin Center → Machines.

"Custom alerts?" → Build Scope + catch with notification action.

"Debug tactic?" → Add Compose actions to inspect expression values.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Run history = step-by-step log of every flow execution
  • Each step shows: status, inputs, outputs, duration, errors
  • Default retention: 28 days free, 90 days premium
  • Resubmit failed runs after fixing transient issues
  • Cancel mid-run if flow stuck or wrong data
  • Flow analytics tab: success rate, run count, errors, duration trends
  • Power Automate Admin Center: tenant-wide flow management and analytics
  • Process Advisor: discover automation opportunities (Task Mining, Process Mining)
  • Audit log: track flow lifecycle events in Microsoft 365 Compliance Center
  • DLP policies in Admin Center: restrict connector combinations
  • Built-in alerts: owner emailed after threshold failures
  • Custom alerts: Scope + Catch with Send email/Teams message
  • Mobile app: notifications for failures and approvals
  • Desktop flow runs visible in Power Automate cloud; full local logs on machine
  • Machine health: monitor online/offline status in Admin Center
  • Best practices: critical alerts immediate, routine digest, audit table, Power BI dashboard, connection health checks

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

This final section covers production governance: DLP policies, environment strategy, CoE (Center of Excellence), naming conventions, ALM, and certification paths. Includes a mock exam to verify PL-100 and PL-500 readiness.

Data Loss Prevention (DLP)

DLP = policies that restrict how connectors can be used together
 Prevents accidental data leaks
 Configured by admins; applied tenant-wide or per-environment

Three connector categories:

Business:
 Used for business-sensitive data
 Examples: Dataverse, SharePoint, Outlook
 Configured per environment

Non-Business:
 Used for personal / non-sensitive data
 Examples: Twitter, RSS, personal email
 Configured per environment

Blocked:
 Cannot be used at all in this environment
 Examples: certain third-party connectors with security concerns

Key rule:
 Connectors in DIFFERENT categories CANNOT be used in same flow
 Business connector + Non-Business connector = blocked
 This prevents: sending corporate data to personal services

Setup:
 Power Platform Admin Center → Data policies → + New policy
 Add connectors to each category
 Apply to: all environments, specific environments, all-except-listed

Best practices:
 - Default everything to Non-Business; opt in to Business for needed ones
 - Block clearly risky connectors (personal email, social media for orgs)
 - Document categorization decisions
 - Review periodically as connectors added

Environment strategy

Environments = containers for Power Platform resources
 Each has its own Dataverse, flows, apps, connections
 Used for: separation, isolation, ALM

Common strategy:

Dev environment:
 Where makers build and test
 May have multiple per team
 Easy to break; isolated from production
 Often has sample/test data

Test/QA environment:
 Higher fidelity to production
 Used for integration testing, UAT
 Cleaner data than Dev

Prod environment:
 Production flows and apps
 Restricted access (only admin can edit)
 Real users, real data
 Strict change control

Default environment:
 Created by Microsoft for each tenant
 Shared by everyone in org
 Limited governance
 Best: don't put production assets here

Sandbox environment:
 Same capacity as Prod but explicitly for testing
 Can be reset
 Often used: pre-deployment validation

License: each environment consumes capacity
Add new environments via Admin Center

Best practices:
 - Use solutions to move flows between environments
 - Don't develop directly in production
 - Limit access to production
 - Use environment variables for env-specific config

Center of Excellence (CoE)

CoE = formal team and toolkit for governing Power Platform adoption

Microsoft CoE Toolkit:
 Free open-source toolkit from Microsoft
 Installable in any tenant
 Provides: dashboards, governance flows, training resources

Components:
 Inventory:
 All flows, apps, makers tracked
 Update timestamps
 Connection usage
 License consumption
 
 Adoption tracking:
 Active makers per month
 Flow run volumes
 Connector usage trends
 
 Governance:
 Auto-disable orphaned flows (owner left)
 Auto-disable flows with no runs in N days
 Auto-archive old flows
 DLP policy compliance checks
 
 Communications:
 Maker newsletter (auto-generated)
 Champion recognition
 Training material distribution

Why CoE matters:
 - Visibility into shadow IT (people building flows without knowing)
 - Compliance and security oversight
 - License optimization (find unused premium licenses)
 - Maker enablement (training, support)

Roles in CoE:
 Executive sponsor
 CoE lead
 Maker champions
 Platform admin
 Compliance liaison

Naming conventions

Consistent naming = critical for governance and maintainability

Flow naming pattern:
 [Type] - [Department] - [Purpose] - [Status]
 
 Examples:
 "Cloud - HR - Onboarding Email Trigger - Production"
 "Desktop - Finance - Invoice Entry - Dev"
 "Scheduled - IT - Daily Disk Cleanup - Production"

Convention examples:
 Prefix by type: CF (Cloud Flow), DF (Desktop Flow), BPF (Business Process Flow)
 Suffix by env: _Dev, _Test, _Prod
 Include team/owner shorthand
 Be descriptive; not "Test Flow 1"

Action naming in flows:
 Rename "Apply to each" to "For each attachment"
 Rename "Compose" to "Compose order summary"
 Rename "Condition" to "Check if priority is high"
 Makes flow self-documenting

Variable naming:
 camelCase or snake_case (be consistent)
 Descriptive: orderTotal, not x
 Boolean prefix: is/has (isProcessed, hasAttachments)

Solution naming:
 PublisherPrefix_SolutionName
 Example: contoso_FinanceOnboarding

Why this matters:
 - Search across hundreds of flows
 - Understand at a glance what each does
 - Easier ownership identification
 - Less risk of accidental modifications

Solutions and ALM

Solutions = portable containers for Power Platform components
 Enable ALM (Application Lifecycle Management)
 Critical for moving between environments

Solution contents:
 Flows
 Apps (Power Apps)
 Custom connectors
 Dataverse tables, columns, relationships
 Environment variables
 Connection references

Solution types:
 Unmanaged: editable; for active development
 Managed: read-only; for deployments

Workflow:
 1. Create solution in Dev environment
 2. Add components to solution
 3. Build and test
 4. Export as managed solution
 5. Import to Test/Prod environment
 6. Components installed; ready to use

Connection references:
 Abstract connection from solution
 Map connection in target environment
 No need to recreate connections per env

Environment variables:
 Config values that change per environment
 E.g., admin email, API endpoint URL
 Set values in each target environment

Pipelines (newer):
 Power Platform Pipelines: managed deployments
 Automate solution export → import → deploy
 Approval gates between stages
 Audit trail of deployments

Best practices:
 - Always use solutions for production work
 - One solution per business area
 - Document component dependencies
 - Test in staging before prod deployment

Sharing and permissions

Sharing flows:
 My flows → click flow → Share
 Add users / groups
 Permissions:
 Owner — full control; can edit, run, share
 Co-owner — same as Owner (but can't delete original)
 User — can run; cannot edit

Sharing implications:
 Connection authentication:
 Embedded: shared users use OWNER's connections
 User-owned: each user must authenticate

 Common pattern:
 Service account owns flow
 Connections use service account credentials
 Users get "Run only" access
 Avoids credential issues

Audit trail:
 Each share action logged
 Compliance review possible
 Cannot share with external users (tenant-only)

Connection types:
 Personal: only one user uses
 Service principal: shared identity (production)
 Premium: required for advanced auth methods

Best practices:
 - Service account for production flows
 - "Run only" for end users (avoids accidental edits)
 - Document sharing policies
 - Audit periodically

Certification paths

Microsoft Power Platform certification ladder:

PL-900: Power Platform Fundamentals
 Entry-level; covers all Power Platform components
 Concepts of Power Apps, Power Automate, Power BI, etc.
 ~$100; ~50 questions; 60 minutes
 Foundation for everything else

PL-100: Power Platform App Maker
 Builds canvas and model-driven apps + simple Power Automate
 Includes: Power Apps, basic Power Automate, basic Dataverse
 ~$165; ~40-60 questions
 This is what you've studied throughout PWR-APPS course

PL-200: Power Platform Functional Consultant
 Deeper: model-driven apps, advanced Dataverse, business process flows
 For functional consultants who configure (not code)
 ~$165

PL-300: Power BI Data Analyst
 Power BI specific
 Covered in your DC-PBI course studies

PL-400: Power Platform Developer
 Code-heavy: custom connectors, plug-ins, scripts, API integration
 Includes Power Fx advanced topics
 ~$165

PL-500: Power Automate RPA Developer
 Desktop flows focused
 Power Automate Desktop in depth
 Recently added; for RPA specialists
 ~$165

PL-600: Power Platform Solution Architect
 Highest individual cert (besides specialized)
 Architecture design across Power Platform
 Multi-tenant scenarios
 ~$165

Recommended study path:
 Start: PL-900 (concepts)
 Next: PL-100 (app making basics)
 Specialize: PL-200 (functional) OR PL-400 (developer)
 Advanced: PL-500 (RPA) OR PL-600 (architect)

Renewal:
 Annual free renewal assessment
 Take after 1 year of certification
 Keeps cert current

Production deployment checklist

Before deploying a flow to production:

Design:
 ☐ Naming follows convention
 ☐ Trigger conditions narrow events to needed only
 ☐ All actions have proper Run After settings
 ☐ Error handling wraps critical sections
 ☐ Failure notifications to right people
 ☐ Idempotent design (safe to retry)

Configuration:
 ☐ Service account used for connections (not personal)
 ☐ Environment variables used for env-specific config
 ☐ No hardcoded credentials/secrets
 ☐ Secrets in Azure Key Vault if applicable
 ☐ Premium licenses verified for all premium connectors

Testing:
 ☐ Happy path tested with realistic data
 ☐ Edge cases tested (empty, null, large)
 ☐ Error scenarios tested (network failure simulation)
 ☐ Performance tested at expected volume
 ☐ Run-time confirmed within SLA

Documentation:
 ☐ Description filled in for flow + key actions
 ☐ Connection requirements documented
 ☐ Trigger event documented
 ☐ Owner / co-owner identified
 ☐ Runbook for support team

Deployment:
 ☐ Package as managed solution
 ☐ Test in staging environment first
 ☐ Verify connection references map correctly
 ☐ Apply DLP policies are compatible
 ☐ Notify stakeholders of deployment

Monitoring:
 ☐ Alerts configured for critical failures
 ☐ Run history reviewed first week post-deploy
 ☐ Performance metrics tracked
 ☐ Cost / license consumption monitored

Mock exam — 15 questions

▸ PL-100 / PL-500 Mock Exam

Test yourself; answers below.

  1. Power Automate was previously called what name?
  2. What are the three types of cloud flows?
  3. Which mode of desktop flow requires a premium license: attended or unattended?
  4. Where does a cloud flow execute?
  5. What action waits for human decision before continuing the flow?
  6. What is the syntax to reference a variable named "Total" in an expression?
  7. What is the difference between Standard and Premium connectors?
  8. Which action provides multi-branch decision based on a single value?
  9. How do you achieve a try-catch pattern in Power Automate?
  10. What is the default retry policy for actions?
  11. What is DLP and what categories does it use?
  12. How does a cloud flow trigger a desktop flow?
  13. What is the maximum number of iterations in a Do until loop by default?
  14. Which file format can you import to create a custom connector?
  15. What does the workflow()?['run/id'] expression return?

Answers:

  1. Microsoft Flow
  2. Automated, Instant, Scheduled
  3. Unattended
  4. In Microsoft's cloud (data centers)
  5. Start and wait for an approval
  6. variables('Total')
  7. Standard is included with M365; Premium requires extra license (Power Automate per User or per Flow)
  8. Switch action
  9. Scope action + configure Run After Failed on a second Scope (catch); + Run After all statuses on third Scope (finally)
  10. Exponential backoff, 4 retries; total ~30 seconds
  11. Data Loss Prevention; categorizes connectors as Business, Non-Business, Blocked; prevents cross-category use
  12. Action: "Run a flow built with Power Automate Desktop"
  13. 60 iterations or 1 hour timeout (whichever first)
  14. OpenAPI/Swagger (YAML or JSON) or Postman collection
  15. The unique run ID of the current flow execution; used for logging/notifications

Additional questions

▸ More practice
  1. What is the purpose of a connection reference in a solution?
  2. Name three M365 standard connectors.
  3. What does the @ symbol indicate in a flow input field?
  4. Inside Apply to each, how do you reference the current item in an expression?
  5. What's the recommended account type for production flow connections: personal or service account?
  6. Which Power Automate plan supports the highest API request limits?
  7. What is Process Advisor used for?
  8. How do you make a flow run only for emails from external senders?
  9. What's the difference between managed and unmanaged solutions?
  10. Which certification focuses specifically on RPA (desktop flows)?

Answers:

  1. Abstracts the connection from a specific environment so the solution can be deployed across multiple environments without recreating connections manually
  2. Office 365 Outlook, SharePoint, Microsoft Teams (or OneDrive, Excel Online, Office 365 Users, Forms, Planner, etc.)
  3. Triggers dynamic content / expression input (older syntax for inserting tokens)
  4. items('Apply_to_each')
  5. Service account — doesn't break when person leaves; consistent identity
  6. Power Automate Premium (per User has highest typical limits)
  7. Discovering automation opportunities through task mining (recording user activities) and process mining (analyzing event logs)
  8. Trigger condition: @not(endsWith(triggerOutputs()?['body/from'], '@yourcompany.com'))
  9. Unmanaged = editable in target environment; Managed = read-only, for production deployments
  10. PL-500 (Power Automate RPA Developer)

Final tips

★ EXAM AND PRODUCTION READINESS
  • Know the three cloud flow types cold: Automated (event), Instant (button), Scheduled (recurrence)
  • Cloud vs Desktop distinction: API vs UI; cloud always preferred when API exists
  • Premium contagion: ANY premium connector makes entire flow premium
  • Expressions are WDL, not Power Fx; key functions: concat, formatDateTime, addDays, if, equals
  • Error handling = Scope + Run After; not try/catch keyword
  • Trigger conditions filter events before flow runs; saves cost
  • Hybrid pattern is the most powerful: cloud orchestration + desktop legacy
  • Solutions for ALM: build in solutions; deploy via managed exports
  • DLP categories: Business, Non-Business, Blocked; never mix Business with Non-Business
  • Idempotency design from day one — saves hours of debugging
  • Monitor proactively: alerts, audit trails, dashboards
  • Service accounts for production; personal for dev only
  • CoE Toolkit for tenant-wide governance
  • Naming conventions from start — critical at scale
  • Test thoroughly: happy path, edge cases, errors, performance
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • DLP (Data Loss Prevention) restricts connector combinations: Business, Non-Business, Blocked categories
  • Environment strategy: Dev, Test/QA, Prod, Sandbox — use solutions to move between
  • CoE (Center of Excellence) provides tenant-wide visibility and governance
  • Microsoft's CoE Toolkit is free and adds dashboards, governance flows, training
  • Naming conventions: descriptive prefixes/suffixes; rename actions for clarity
  • Solutions = portable containers for ALM; managed (read-only) for production
  • Connection references abstract connections for cross-environment deployments
  • Environment variables hold config that changes per env (URLs, IDs, emails)
  • Sharing: Owner (full), Co-owner (edit + share), User (run only)
  • Service accounts recommended for production (over personal accounts)
  • Certification ladder: PL-900 (fundamentals) → PL-100 (app maker) → PL-200/400 → PL-500 (RPA) → PL-600 (architect)
  • PL-100 covers Power Apps + basic Power Automate
  • PL-500 covers Power Automate Desktop / RPA in depth
  • Production checklist: naming, error handling, service accounts, secrets in Key Vault, monitoring
  • Process Advisor finds automation opportunities through Task Mining and Process Mining
  • This completes the Power Automate course — you're ready for PL-100 and PL-500 mocks

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

📋 Power Automate Overview

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Introduction to Power Automate

▸ Power Automate is Microsoft's automation platform — formerly called Microsoft Flow. It connects services, automates repetitive tasks, and ranges from simple email triggers to enterprise RPA. The PL-100, PL-200, and PL-500 exams all test…

▸ Power Automate = Microsoft's low-code automation platform History: Originally called "Microsoft Flow" (2016) Renamed to "Power Automate" in 2019 What it does: - Trigger workflows on events (email arrives, item created, scheduled time) -…

Cloud Flows vs Desktop Flows

▸ Power Automate has two distinct execution models: cloud flows (running on Microsoft's servers, talking to APIs) and desktop flows (running on a Windows PC, controlling the UI). They solve different problems. The PL-100 and PL-500 exams…

▸ Cloud flows run in Microsoft's data centers Architecture: Trigger (event) → Power Automate cloud → Actions (API calls) No local installation needed Connect to: Cloud services with APIs (Microsoft 365, Salesforce, ServiceNow, etc.) REST…

Triggers and Actions

▸ Triggers and actions are the atoms of any flow. Every flow has exactly one trigger and one or more actions. The PL-100 exam tests recognizing trigger types, common actions, and their configuration patterns.

▸ Some connectors don't support push notifications Power Automate "polls" the service periodically Example: SharePoint "When an item is created" Power Automate checks the list every 5-15 seconds (free tier; faster on premium) Compares last poll's results with the current state and fires the trigger for anything new — which is why polling triggers can lag a few seconds and premium plans poll faster.

Approval Flows

▸ Approvals are one of Power Automate's most powerful built-in features. They wait for human decisions, integrate with email and Teams, and resume the flow based on the response. The PL-100 exam tests approval types, responses, and…

▸ Approval = built-in step that PAUSES a flow until a person makes a decision Use cases: - Expense approval (manager signs off on submission) - Document review (peer review before publish) - Leave request (HR approves time-off) - Purchase orders (finance approves spend over a threshold). The flow pauses at the approval action and resumes on the response — branch on Approve/Reject to handle each outcome.

Microsoft 365 Connectors

▸ Microsoft 365 connectors are the workhorses of Power Automate — Outlook, SharePoint, Teams, OneDrive, Excel, Planner, Forms. Every M365 customer can use these without premium licensing. The PL-100 exam tests common operations on these…

Custom Connectors

▸ When no built-in connector exists for the service you need, custom connectors are the answer. They wrap any REST API so you can use it like a first-class connector across all your flows and apps. The PL-100 exam tests recognizing when to…

📋 Expressions and Logic

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Dynamic Content

▸ Dynamic content is how a flow's actions consume the outputs of earlier steps — trigger data, action results, variables. Without it, every flow would be a series of hardcoded steps. Understanding tokens vs expressions is critical for PL-100.

▸ Dynamic content = values from previous steps available to current step How it appears: Click in any input field of an action Right-side panel slides open with "Dynamic content" tab Lists all outputs from earlier steps Click any item →…

Expressions and Functions

▸ Power Automate has its own expression language (Workflow Definition Language / WDL) — different from Power Fx in Power Apps. When dynamic content alone isn't enough, expressions handle transformations: concat strings, format dates, compute…

▸ Expressions = function-based formulas evaluated at runtime Different from Power Fx (Power Apps) Based on Workflow Definition Language (WDL) When to use: - Transform values (uppercase, format dates, etc.) - Math operations - Conditional…

Conditions and Switches

▸ Real flows branch — "if email contains 'urgent' then escalate, else file in archive." Power Automate gives you two branching actions: Condition (two-way) and Switch (multi-way). Knowing when to use which keeps flows readable instead of…

▸ Condition action (Control > Condition): Evaluates ONE comparison (or compound) → splits into 2 branches Layout: [Trigger] [Condition: Status == "Active"] ├─ If yes │ [Actions for yes branch] └─ If no [Actions for no branch] Builder fields:…

Loops: Apply to Each and Do Until

▸ Real automation processes lots of things at once — "for every new file in this folder, send a confirmation," "for each row in a CSV, create a record." Power Automate has two loop actions: Apply to each (iterate a known array) and Do until…

▸ Apply to each (Control > Apply to each): Iterates over an ARRAY (collection) Runs the inner actions ONCE per element Inputs: Any array — from a List action, parsed JSON, split string, etc. Examples: - List rows present in table → returns an array of rows - Get response details → array of form answers. Tip: large loops are slow by default — turn on concurrency control when order doesn't matter.

📋 Desktop Flows and RPA

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Power Automate Desktop

▸ Cloud flows can't click buttons in legacy desktop apps, fill in PDF forms, or operate SAP. Enter Power Automate Desktop (PAD) — Microsoft's free RPA tool for Windows. PAD records and automates ANYTHING a user does on a Windows machine.…

▸ Power Automate Desktop (PAD): Windows desktop application for RPA (Robotic Process Automation) Records and runs scripts that automate UI and apps Free with Windows 10/11 (included since Windows 11) Use cases: - Automate legacy desktop apps…

UI Automation

▸ The heart of RPA is UI automation — telling the robot exactly which button to click, which field to type into. Getting selectors right is the #1 skill that separates flows that work for 5 minutes from flows that run reliably for years.…

▸ In PAD: Actions panel → UI automation Subcategories: Data extraction: Get details of UI element, Get details of window Form filling: Click UI element, Populate text field, Press button Selection: Select menu option, Set checkbox, Set radio…

Web Automation

▸ Web automation in Power Automate Desktop handles tasks against websites — scraping data, filling forms, navigating pages. It's essential when a service has no API but exposes a web UI. The PL-500 exam tests browser automation patterns.

▸ Power Automate Desktop supports automation in: - Microsoft Edge (built-in) - Google Chrome (extension required) - Mozilla Firefox (extension required) - Internet Explorer (legacy; deprecated) Browser extensions: Install during PAD setup,…

Combining Cloud and Desktop

Pattern 1: Cloud-orchestrated legacy data entry — Trigger: SharePoint item created (cloud) Cloud Actions: Get item details Look up customer in cloud CRM Determine if legacy entry needed If yes: Run desktop flow:…

Pattern 2: Scheduled batch with desktop — Trigger: Recurrence nightly at 2am (cloud) Cloud Actions: Get list of pending records from Dataverse For each record: Run desktop flow: ProcessOneRecord Pass record…

Pattern 3: Approval triggers desktop — Trigger: PowerApps button (cloud) Cloud Actions: Start approval (manager approval) Wait for response If approved: Run desktop flow: ProcessApproved Pass: approved item details as input variables. The pattern: the cloud flow owns triggers and approvals, the desktop flow does the legacy-app clicks, and input/output variables bridge the two.

📋 Operations and Best Practices

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Error Handling and Retries

▸ Production flows fail — API errors, throttling, timeouts, bad data. Without error handling, a flow either silently corrupts data or stops running. Power Automate's error handling patterns are tested on the PL-100 and PL-500 exams.

▸ Action statuses after running: Succeeded — completed normally Failed — error during execution Skipped — Run After conditions not met Timed out — exceeded action timeout Cancelled — flow was cancelled mid-run Common failure causes:…

Monitoring and Logs

▸ Once flows run in production, you need to know they're working — and quickly find out when they're not. Power Automate provides run history, analytics, Process Advisor, and admin dashboards. The PL-100 and PL-500 exams test monitoring…

▸ Run history = log of every flow execution Access: make.powerautomate.com → My flows → click flow → 28-day history (default) Filter by: All / Running / Succeeded / Failed / Cancelled Each run shows: Start time Duration Status Trigger event — and clicking a run reveals every action's inputs and outputs, the fastest way to debug a failed flow.

Governance and Best Practices

Governance essentials — Use environments (dev/test/prod) with DLP policies that control which connectors can be combined; keep flows in solutions for ALM; run production flows under service accounts so they don't die when an employee leaves.

Best practices — Name flows descriptively, add error handling with run-after conditions, avoid infinite trigger loops (a flow that updates the same list that triggers it), and review run history regularly for silent failures.
